front: Which findings in a client with low back pain suggest cauda equina syndrome, and what is the first action?
back: Saddle anesthesia, new bladder retention or overflow incontinence, bowel dysfunction, and progressive bilateral leg weakness. This is a surgical emergency, so stop the examination and arrange immediate emergency referral.

front: Which history items raise suspicion of a spinal fracture as the cause of low back pain?
back: Major trauma, minor trauma in an older or osteoporotic client, prolonged corticosteroid use, and age over 70. Fracture risk rises with each item, so screen for these before loading the spine.

front: List the screening red flags for spinal malignancy in a client with low back pain.
back: Past history of cancer, unexplained weight loss, age over 50, constant night pain unrelieved by rest or position, and failure to improve after about one month of appropriate care. Several together warrant medical referral.

front: Which questions screen for spinal infection in a client with low back pain?
back: Ask about fever or chills, a recent bacterial infection, intravenous drug use, immunosuppression, and recent spinal surgery or injection. Constant pain with these features needs prompt medical assessment.

front: Which presentation of back pain should make you suspect an abdominal aortic aneurysm?
back: An older male smoker with deep, throbbing, non-mechanical back or abdominal pain, possibly with a pulsatile abdominal mass. Movement does not change the pain. Refer urgently, because rupture is life-threatening.

front: Match the lumbar myotomes to their test movements: L2, L3, L4, L5, S1.
back: L2 hip flexion, L3 knee extension, L4 ankle dorsiflexion, L5 great toe extension, S1 ankle plantarflexion (or heel raise). Test bilaterally and compare for subtle weakness.

front: Which deep tendon reflexes assess the lumbosacral nerve roots, and what root does each reflect?
back: The patellar reflex reflects L3 and L4, and the Achilles reflex reflects S1 (S1 and S2). A reduced reflex supports a root lesion at that level, but absence can be normal in older adults.

front: What is a positive straight leg raise, and what does it suggest?
back: Reproduction of the client's leg symptoms between roughly 30 and 70 degrees of hip flexion, increased by dorsiflexion. It is sensitive but not specific for lumbar disc herniation with nerve root irritation. A positive crossed test is more specific.

front: Describe the slump test and what makes it positive.
back: The client sits slumped, flexes the neck, then extends the knee and dorsiflexes the ankle. It is positive when symptoms are reproduced and ease when neck flexion is released, indicating neural tissue mechanosensitivity.

front: Which skin areas are used to test L4, L5 and S1 dermatomes?
back: L4 the medial leg and medial malleolus, L5 the dorsum of the foot including the great toe web space, S1 the lateral border of the foot. Compare light touch side to side.

front: Under the Canadian C-spine rule, which three high-risk factors mandate radiography?
back: Age 65 or older, a dangerous mechanism of injury, or paresthesias in the extremities. If any is present, radiography is required before cervical range of motion is assessed.

front: Which low-risk factors allow safe cervical range-of-motion assessment under the Canadian C-spine rule?
back: Simple rear-end collision, sitting in the emergency department, ambulatory at any time, delayed onset of neck pain, and no midline cervical tenderness. If present, test whether the client can actively rotate 45 degrees each way.

front: What are the four items of the Wainner cluster for cervical radiculopathy?
back: Positive Spurling A test, positive distraction test, positive upper limb tension test A, and ipsilateral cervical rotation under 60 degrees. Three of four positive raises probability, and all four positive makes it high.

front: Name the symptoms that suggest cervical arterial dysfunction and the correct response.
back: The 5 Ds and 3 Ns: dizziness, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, drop attacks, nausea, numbness, nystagmus, plus sudden severe unfamiliar headache or neck pain. Stop treatment and arrange urgent medical assessment.

front: Which upper motor neuron signs support cervical myelopathy?
back: Hyperreflexia, positive Hoffmann sign, inverted supinator sign, clonus, positive Babinski, gait disturbance and hand clumsiness. These signs indicate spinal cord compression and call for prompt medical referral.

front: How does a costovertebral joint or rib dysfunction typically present?
back: Localized unilateral thoracic or rib pain that is sharp with deep inspiration, coughing or trunk rotation, with tenderness over the joint and reproduction on rib springing. Rule out cardiopulmonary causes first.

front: Which features make thoracic or chest pain suspicious for a cardiac cause?
back: Pressure or heaviness that spreads to the left arm or jaw, brought on by exertion, with sweating, nausea or shortness of breath, and unchanged by movement or palpation. Call emergency services without delay.

front: Describe the rib motion pattern of the upper ribs versus the lower ribs during breathing.
back: Upper ribs (1 to 6) move in a pump-handle pattern, increasing anteroposterior chest diameter. Lower ribs (7 to 10) move in a bucket-handle pattern, increasing transverse diameter. Ribs 11 and 12 move in a caliper pattern.

front: Which visceral condition refers pain to the right shoulder or interscapular area and relates to meals?
back: Gallbladder disease. Pain follows fatty meals, may come with nausea, and does not change with spinal movement or palpation. A mechanical examination that fails to reproduce the pain should prompt medical referral.

front: What is the commonly cited normal range of thoracic kyphosis and a rigid, severe kyphosis in an adolescent suggests what?
back: Normal thoracic kyphosis is commonly cited as about 20 to 40 degrees. A rigid, angular kyphosis that does not correct on extension in an adolescent suggests Scheuermann disease.

front: What does a painful arc suggest in shoulder assessment?
back: Pain during mid-range arm elevation, roughly 60 to 120 degrees of abduction, that eases above and below that range. It suggests subacromial pain syndrome, with compression of the rotator cuff or bursa under the acromion.

front: How is the empty can (Jobe) test performed and which muscle does it test?
back: The arm is elevated to 90 degrees in the scapular plane, thumb pointing down, then resisted downward pressure is applied. Pain or weakness suggests supraspinatus tendinopathy or tear.

front: What does a positive drop arm test indicate?
back: The client cannot lower the abducted arm slowly from 90 degrees or the arm drops suddenly. It indicates a large full-thickness rotator cuff tear, most often involving supraspinatus.

front: What is the Park cluster for subacromial impingement?
back: Three tests: positive Hawkins-Kennedy test, positive painful arc, and weakness on resisted external rotation (infraspinatus test). When all three are positive, the likelihood of subacromial impingement rises substantially.

front: Which tests assess infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis?
back: Resisted external rotation with the arm at the side tests infraspinatus. The Hornblower sign tests teres minor. The lift-off test or belly press test assesses subscapularis.

front: What is the capsular pattern of the glenohumeral joint?
back: External rotation is most limited, then abduction, then internal rotation. A capsular pattern with painful, restricted passive movement suggests adhesive capsulitis or joint arthritis rather than a muscle problem.

front: Describe the stages and typical client for adhesive capsulitis.
back: Painful freezing stage, then stiff frozen stage, then thawing stage. It is most common in people aged 40 to 60, more often women, and is strongly associated with diabetes.

front: How do the apprehension and relocation tests identify anterior shoulder instability?
back: Supine, the arm is placed in 90 degrees abduction and external rotation, and apprehension is a positive sign. A posteriorly directed force then reduces the apprehension, which is the positive relocation test.

front: What does a positive sulcus sign indicate?
back: A visible gap below the acromion when inferior traction is applied to the arm at the side. It indicates inferior glenohumeral laxity and is a hallmark of multidirectional instability.

front: How is the O'Brien active compression test performed for a SLAP lesion?
back: The arm is flexed to 90 degrees, adducted 10 degrees, and internally rotated with the thumb down. Resisted elevation causes pain that is reduced with the palm up. Diagnostic accuracy is limited, so interpret with the history.

front: Which findings support lateral epicondylalgia (tennis elbow)?
back: Pain over the lateral epicondyle on resisted wrist and finger extension (Cozen test) or gripping, with local tenderness over the common extensor origin. The extensor carpi radialis brevis tendon is most often involved.

front: List the five items of the Wainner carpal tunnel syndrome cluster.
back: Shaking the hands relieves symptoms, wrist ratio index over 0.67, symptom severity scale over 1.9, reduced median sensation in the thumb, and age over 45. Four of five positive makes carpal tunnel syndrome likely.

front: Which structures are involved in De Quervain tenosynovitis and what test is used?
back: Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis in the first dorsal compartment. Pain at the radial styloid is reproduced by the Finkelstein test: thumb in the fist, then ulnar deviation of the wrist.

front: What is Froment sign and which nerve does it indicate?
back: When asked to hold a sheet of paper between thumb and index finger, the client flexes the thumb interphalangeal joint to compensate. It shows weak adductor pollicis and indicates an ulnar nerve lesion.

front: How is Phalen test performed and what is a positive result?
back: The wrists are held in full flexion, backs of the hands together, for up to 60 seconds. Reproduction of numbness or tingling in the median nerve distribution suggests carpal tunnel syndrome.

front: How is the FADIR test performed and how should a positive result be interpreted?
back: The hip is flexed, adducted and internally rotated. Groin pain is a positive result. The test is sensitive for femoroacetabular impingement or intra-articular pathology but not specific, so correlate with the rest of the examination.

front: What is the typical capsular pattern of hip osteoarthritis?
back: Internal rotation is limited first and most, followed by flexion and abduction. A painful, stiff hip with restricted internal rotation in an older client suggests osteoarthritis.

front: How do cam and pincer femoroacetabular impingement differ?
back: Cam impingement is a bump at the femoral head-neck junction, typically in young active males. Pincer impingement is acetabular overcoverage, more often in middle-aged women. Many people have a combined pattern.

front: What does a positive Trendelenburg sign show?
back: When standing on one leg, the pelvis drops on the opposite, unsupported side. It indicates weakness of the gluteus medius on the stance side, or a superior gluteal nerve problem.

front: Which findings support greater trochanteric pain syndrome?
back: Lateral hip pain with tenderness over the greater trochanter, pain lying on the affected side, and pain reproduced by single leg stance held for about 30 seconds. Gluteal tendinopathy is a common cause.

front: Why is the Lachman test preferred for assessing the anterior cruciate ligament?
back: With the knee at 20 to 30 degrees of flexion, anterior tibial translation with a soft end feel is assessed. It is the most sensitive ACL test and is easier than the anterior drawer in an acute, swollen knee.

front: What does the pivot shift test detect and what is a positive sign?
back: Anterolateral rotatory instability from ACL deficiency. With valgus and internal rotation as the knee flexes from extension, the tibia subluxes and then reduces with a clunk at about 20 to 40 degrees. It is highly specific.

front: How do you perform the posterior drawer test and which ligament does it assess?
back: With the knee at 90 degrees, a posterior force is applied to the proximal tibia. Excessive posterior translation indicates posterior cruciate ligament injury, and a posterior sag sign supports it.

front: Which collateral ligaments do valgus and varus stress tests assess, and why test at 0 and 30 degrees?
back: Valgus stress tests the medial collateral ligament and varus stress tests the lateral collateral ligament. Laxity at 30 degrees is isolated collateral injury. Laxity also at 0 degrees suggests additional cruciate or posterior capsule damage.

front: State the Ottawa knee rule criteria for radiography.
back: Radiography is needed with age 55 or older, isolated patellar tenderness, fibular head tenderness, inability to flex to 90 degrees, or inability to bear weight for four steps both immediately and in the emergency department.

front: Which history and examination findings suggest a meniscal tear?
back: Joint line tenderness, mechanical symptoms such as catching or locking, delayed swelling after a twisting injury, and pain with deep squatting. Joint line tenderness is sensitive, while locking is more specific.

front: How is the Thessaly test performed and what is a positive result?
back: The client stands on the affected leg with the knee flexed about 20 degrees and rotates the body in and out three times. Joint line pain or a locking or catching sensation suggests a meniscal tear.

front: What is the J sign in patellar tracking?
back: Abrupt lateral deviation of the patella near terminal knee extension, tracing a J shape. It suggests maltracking with lateral patellar displacement, often from weak vastus medialis or tight lateral structures.

front: How does infrapatellar fat pad impingement present?
back: Anterior knee pain with tenderness on both sides of the patellar tendon, worse with end-range knee extension or prolonged standing. Pain reproduction with tendon-sided palpation and passive hyperextension supports Hoffa fat pad syndrome.

front: What does a positive patellar apprehension test indicate?
back: With the knee slightly flexed, a lateral glide of the patella provokes apprehension or quadriceps contraction. It indicates patellar instability, commonly after a previous lateral dislocation.

front: According to the Ottawa ankle rules, when is an ankle radiograph series indicated in a patient with malleolar zone pain?
back: Bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus (distal 6 cm), or inability to bear weight for four steps both immediately after injury and at assessment.

front: Which findings call for a foot (midfoot) radiograph under the Ottawa ankle rules?
back: Midfoot pain plus bone tenderness at the base of the fifth metatarsal or at the navicular, or inability to bear weight for four steps. The rules are highly sensitive, so a negative result safely rules out fracture.

front: How is a lateral ankle sprain graded I, II and III?
back: Grade I: mild stretch, minimal swelling, no laxity. Grade II: partial tear, moderate swelling and bruising, mild to moderate laxity. Grade III: complete rupture, marked swelling and instability, often loss of function.

front: How is the Thompson test performed and interpreted?
back: With the patient prone and the foot over the table edge, squeeze the calf. Absent or reduced plantarflexion compared with the other side indicates a complete Achilles tendon rupture.

front: What is the classic presentation of plantar fasciopathy (plantar heel pain)?
back: Sharp pain with the first steps in the morning or after rest, easing then returning with load. Tenderness is at the medial calcaneal tubercle, and the windlass test (passive great toe extension) may reproduce it.

front: What is the Laslett cluster for sacroiliac joint pain?
back: Three or more positive pain provocation tests from distraction, thigh thrust, compression, sacral thrust and Gaenslen tests. The cluster has good accuracy for identifying the SIJ as a pain source.

front: How is the thigh thrust test for the SIJ performed?
back: Patient supine with the hip flexed to 90 degrees. The examiner applies a posteriorly directed force through the femur, stressing the SIJ. Reproduction of the familiar buttock pain is positive.

front: Where does the patient point to in the Fortin finger test, and what does it suggest?
back: The patient points with one finger to pain just inferior and medial to the posterior superior iliac spine. A single-finger point within about 1 cm suggests the SIJ as the source.

front: How does centralization of symptoms with repeated movements help separate lumbar from SIJ pain?
back: Centralization with repeated lumbar movements points to a lumbar discogenic source. SIJ pain does not centralize and is instead reproduced by SIJ provocation tests.

front: How can hip joint pain be distinguished from SIJ or buttock pain at assessment?
back: Hip pathology gives groin pain, painful limited internal rotation, and a positive FADIR test. SIJ pain is usually buttock pain below L5, with a positive provocation cluster and normal hip range.

front: What features suggest a tibial stress fracture in a runner?
back: Localized bony tenderness, pain that builds with impact activity and eases with rest, and pain with the hop test. Early radiographs are often normal, so MRI is the most sensitive imaging.

front: Why is a femoral neck stress fracture treated as high risk, and what is the first action?
back: It can displace and cause avascular necrosis. Suspect it with groin pain on hopping or weight bearing, stop loading, and arrange urgent medical referral with protected weight bearing.

front: What are the key signs of a scaphoid fracture after a fall on an outstretched hand?
back: Tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox and pain on axial compression of the thumb. The first radiograph may be normal, so immobilize and arrange repeat imaging or MRI.

front: What is the typical limb position and finding in a displaced hip fracture?
back: The leg is shortened and externally rotated, with groin pain and inability to bear weight. This needs emergency medical transfer, and the patient should not be walked.

front: Which risk factors raise suspicion of osteoporosis and fragility fracture risk?
back: Prior fragility fracture, older age, long-term glucocorticoid use, low body weight, parental hip fracture, smoking and heavy alcohol use. Risk tools such as FRAX combine these with bone density.

front: How are muscle strains graded I to III?
back: Grade I: few fibres torn, mild pain, no real strength loss. Grade II: partial tear with moderate pain, swelling and weakness. Grade III: complete rupture with major weakness and often a palpable gap.

front: Which findings suggest acute compartment syndrome, and what is the first action?
back: Pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, and a tense swollen limb. Pulselessness is a late sign. Remove tight bandages and arrange emergency medical referral for fasciotomy assessment.

front: When does delayed onset muscle soreness typically peak, and what causes it?
back: It peaks 24 to 72 hours after unaccustomed or eccentric exercise, from microscopic muscle damage. Pain is diffuse and tender on palpation, and strength recovers within about a week.

front: Which warning signs after intense exertion suggest rhabdomyolysis?
back: Severe muscle pain and swelling, marked weakness, and dark tea-coloured urine. Creatine kinase is very high, and the risk is kidney injury, so refer urgently for medical care.

front: What presentation after a thigh contusion suggests myositis ossificans?
back: A firm, tender mass with increasing pain and falling range of motion weeks after a deep contusion. Avoid aggressive massage and passive stretching early, and refer for imaging if suspected.

front: How is manual muscle test grade 3 defined?
back: The muscle moves the joint through full available range against gravity but cannot tolerate any added resistance. Grade 4 tolerates moderate resistance, and grade 5 is normal strength.

front: What are manual muscle test grades 2, 1 and 0?
back: Grade 2: full range with gravity eliminated. Grade 1: palpable or visible contraction without joint movement. Grade 0: no contraction detected at all.

front: How is a universal goniometer aligned to measure joint range?
back: Centre the axis over the joint axis, align the stationary arm with the proximal segment, and align the moving arm with the distal segment. Use bony landmarks and consistent patient positioning.

front: How do you calculate the minimal detectable change from the standard error of measurement?
back: MDC95 = 1.96 x square root of 2 x SEM. A change smaller than the MDC may be measurement error rather than true change in the patient.

front: In hand-held dynamometry, how do make and break tests differ?
back: In a make test the patient pushes against a fixed examiner resistance. In a break test the examiner overcomes the contraction. Break tests give higher values and more risk of injury, so use one method consistently.

front: What are the main passive end-feel types, and which one suggests acute pathology?
back: Hard (bone on bone), soft (tissue approximation), firm (capsule or ligament stretch), and empty. An empty end-feel means pain stops movement before tissue resistance, suggesting acute inflammation or serious pathology.

front: What is the capsular pattern at the glenohumeral joint?
back: External rotation is most limited, then abduction, then internal rotation. A capsular pattern points to a joint-wide problem such as adhesive capsulitis or arthritis.

front: What does a non-capsular pattern of restriction suggest?
back: A mechanical or localized cause such as ligament sprain, loose body, internal derangement or muscle lesion. Only some motions are limited, in a pattern not matching the joint's capsular proportions.

front: How are Maitland mobilization grades I to IV defined?
back: Grades I and II are small and large amplitude oscillations in the free range, without tissue resistance. Grades III and IV are large and small amplitude oscillations into resistance. Grade V is a thrust.

front: What does the Beighton score measure, and how many points are available?
back: Generalized joint hypermobility, scored out of 9 (little finger extension, thumb to forearm, elbow and knee hyperextension, and palms to floor). Cut-offs vary by age, commonly 5 or more in younger adults.

front: What is the scoring range and minimal clinically important difference for the LEFS?
back: Twenty items scored 0 to 4 give a maximum of 80, where higher means better function. The minimal clinically important difference is 9 scale points.

front: How is the DASH scored, and does a higher score mean better or worse function?
back: The 30-item DASH is scored from 0 to 100, and a higher score means greater disability. The QuickDASH uses 11 items. Minimal clinically important change is roughly 10 points.

front: What does the Neck Disability Index (NDI) consist of and how is it interpreted?
back: Ten sections scored 0 to 5, for a maximum of 50, often reported as a percentage. A higher score means greater neck-related disability.

front: What is the Oswestry Disability Index and what change is considered meaningful?
back: A 10-section low back pain disability questionnaire scored as a percentage from 0 to 100, where higher means worse. A change of about 10 points is commonly considered clinically important.

front: How does the Patient-Specific Functional Scale (PSFS) work?
back: The patient names three to five important activities they struggle with and rates each from 0 (unable) to 10 (able at pre-injury level). Averaging gives the score, and a 2 point change is meaningful.

front: What are the typical findings in scapular dyskinesis?
back: Prominence of the medial border or inferior angle, early or excessive elevation (shrug), and rapid downward rotation on lowering the arm. Winging with a push-up suggests serratus anterior weakness or long thoracic nerve palsy.

front: What is seen in a Trendelenburg gait, and which muscle is weak?
back: The pelvis drops on the side opposite to the stance leg because the stance-side gluteus medius is weak. A compensated version shows a trunk lean over the weak side.

front: What causes a steppage gait, and which nerve is commonly involved?
back: Dorsiflexor weakness causes foot drop, so the patient lifts the knee high to clear the toes. A common cause is common peroneal nerve injury or an L4 to L5 radiculopathy.

front: What gait speed is a useful warning threshold in older adults?
back: Walking speed below about 0.8 m/s is linked to a higher risk of falls, disability, hospitalization and mortality. Gait speed is often called the sixth vital sign.

front: How is the Functional Movement Screen scored?
back: Seven movement patterns are each scored from 0 to 3, for a maximum of 21. A score of 0 is given when pain occurs during the movement, which needs further clinical assessment.

front: Which signs suggest central sensitization in a patient with chronic pain?
back: Pain out of proportion to the injury, diffuse or non-anatomical spread, allodynia, hyperalgesia, and sensitivity to light, sound or stress. The Central Sensitization Inventory screens for it, with 40 as a common cut-off.

front: What are yellow flags?
back: Psychosocial risk factors for chronicity, such as fear avoidance, catastrophizing, depression, belief that pain means harm, low recovery expectations and passive coping. They are addressed alongside physical treatment.

front: How does the STarT Back Screening Tool stratify risk?
back: Nine items. A total of 3 or less is low risk. A total of 4 or more is medium risk, or high risk if the 5-item psychosocial subscale is 4 or more.

front: What three components does the Pain Catastrophizing Scale measure?
back: Rumination, magnification and helplessness, across 13 items scored 0 to 52. A total of 30 or more is commonly considered clinically relevant catastrophizing.

front: What is the core message of pain neuroscience education?
back: Pain is a protective output of the brain, not a direct measure of tissue damage. Understanding this reduces threat and fear, and supports graded activity and movement.

front: What is the typical joint pattern and stiffness in rheumatoid arthritis?
back: Symmetrical polyarthritis of small joints (MCP, PIP, wrists, MTP), sparing the DIP joints, with morning stiffness lasting longer than 60 minutes and warm swollen joints.

front: What clinical features suggest inflammatory back pain from ankylosing spondylitis?
back: Insidious onset before age 40, morning stiffness over 30 minutes, night pain, and improvement with exercise but not rest. Chest expansion under 2.5 cm and reduced modified Schober increase are typical findings.

front: What is the classic presentation of acute gout?
back: Sudden severe monoarthritis, often of the first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra), with hot, red, exquisitely tender swelling. Crystals in joint fluid are needle-shaped and negatively birefringent.

front: Which features point to psoriatic arthritis rather than rheumatoid arthritis?
back: Dactylitis (sausage digit), DIP joint involvement, nail pitting, enthesitis such as Achilles insertion pain, and an asymmetric joint pattern in a patient with psoriasis.

front: Which features suggest systemic lupus erythematosus in a patient with joint pain?
back: Malar (butterfly) rash, photosensitivity, fatigue, oral ulcers, and non-erosive symmetrical arthralgia, often in a young woman. Kidney involvement is serious, and exercise is adjusted during flares.

front: Which ACR clinical criteria support a diagnosis of knee osteoarthritis without imaging or labs?
back: Knee pain plus at least 3 of 6: age over 50, morning stiffness under 30 minutes, crepitus, bony tenderness, bony enlargement, and no palpable warmth.

front: How does morning stiffness help separate osteoarthritis from inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis?
back: Osteoarthritis stiffness usually settles within 30 minutes. Inflammatory arthritis stiffness typically lasts over 60 minutes, often with swelling and systemic fatigue, which should prompt referral for medical workup.

front: Which hip motions are lost first in hip osteoarthritis, and which passive test is most provocative?
back: Internal rotation is usually lost first, followed by flexion and abduction (capsular pattern). Passive internal rotation, especially at 90 degrees of hip flexion, commonly reproduces groin pain.

front: What is the capsular pattern of the knee, and what does it suggest?
back: Flexion is limited more than extension. It indicates an arthritic or capsular problem such as osteoarthritis, as opposed to a mechanical block like a displaced meniscal tear.

front: A client with knee osteoarthritis reports a sudden flare with a large warm effusion and fever. What should you consider?
back: Septic arthritis or crystal arthropathy (gout, pseudogout). A hot, swollen joint with fever is not a routine osteoarthritis flare and needs same day medical referral.

front: What is the difference between phantom limb sensation and phantom limb pain after amputation?
back: Phantom sensation is painless awareness of the missing limb (tingling, position, itch). Phantom pain is a painful sensation felt in the absent limb, often burning, cramping, or shooting.

front: Which K-level describes a limited community ambulator able to negotiate low-level barriers such as curbs and stairs?
back: K2. K1 is level surface household ambulation at fixed cadence, K3 is variable cadence and most barriers, and K4 is high-impact or high-demand activity such as sport or children.

front: Which K-level applies to a prosthetic user with high-impact demands, such as an athlete or active child?
back: K4. These users exceed basic ambulation skills and need high-energy storing components. K0 means no ability or potential to ambulate or transfer safely, so a prosthesis is not indicated.

front: A residual limb has a very tender, focal point and a positive Tinel sign over the cut nerve end. What is suspected?
back: A symptomatic neuroma. Pressure from the socket can trigger sharp, shooting pain along the nerve. Management includes socket modification and referral for medical or surgical review if pain persists.

front: What does pistoning of the residual limb in the socket usually indicate?
back: Poor suspension or loss of limb volume (shrinkage). Excess vertical movement causes friction and skin breakdown, so check sock ply, liner fit, and suspension before referring to the prosthetist.

front: How do Ortolani and Barlow maneuvers differ in screening an infant for developmental hip dysplasia?
back: Ortolani reduces a dislocated hip into the socket (abduct and lift, felt as a clunk). Barlow provokes dislocation of an unstable hip (adduct with posterior pressure).

front: What is the typical presentation of Legg-Calve-Perthes disease?
back: A boy aged about 4 to 8 with a painless or mildly painful limp, often with referred thigh or knee pain, and limited hip abduction and internal rotation. It is avascular necrosis of the femoral head.

front: What are the classic features of slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE)?
back: An overweight adolescent (about 10 to 16 years) with hip or referred knee pain, limited internal rotation, and obligatory external rotation on passive hip flexion. Refer urgently and keep non-weight-bearing.

front: What does a positive Adams forward bend test show, and what does it indicate?
back: A rib or paraspinal prominence on one side when bending forward. It indicates vertebral rotation, meaning a structural scoliosis, and warrants imaging and referral rather than observation alone.

front: What Cobb angle on standing radiograph defines scoliosis?
back: 10 degrees or more of lateral spinal curvature. The Cobb angle is measured between the most tilted vertebrae at the curve ends and guides monitoring, bracing, and surgical decisions.

front: What is the difference between stress urinary incontinence and urge urinary incontinence?
back: Stress incontinence is leakage with raised abdominal pressure (cough, sneeze, jump). Urge incontinence is leakage preceded by a sudden, hard-to-delay urge, typically linked to overactive bladder.

front: What information does a bladder diary record, and for how long is it typically kept?
back: Fluid intake, voiding times and volumes, urgency, leaks, and triggers, usually over 3 days. It objectively shows frequency, nocturia, and fluid habits that guide the treatment plan.

front: How do cystocele and rectocele differ on examination of pelvic organ prolapse?
back: Cystocele is descent of the bladder into the anterior vaginal wall. Rectocele is bulging of the rectum into the posterior vaginal wall. Both are graded on straining or bearing down.

front: How is pelvic floor muscle strength graded on the modified Oxford scale?
back: 0 to 5: 0 no contraction, 1 flicker, 2 weak, 3 moderate with some lift, 4 good with resisted lift, 5 strong with firm resistance and lift against pressure.

front: During palpation, what finding indicates an incorrect pelvic floor muscle contraction strategy?
back: Bearing down (perineal descent) or gluteal, abdominal, or breath-holding substitution instead of an inward and upward squeeze and lift. Retrain with feedback before progressing strengthening.

front: What are the Kocher criteria for predicting septic arthritis of the hip in a child?
back: Non-weight-bearing on the affected side, ESR over 40 mm/h, fever over 38.5 C, and WBC over 12,000 per microlitre. More positives raise the probability sharply.

front: A hot, swollen joint with fever and severe pain on any movement is present. What is the action?
back: Suspect septic arthritis, a surgical emergency. Do not treat. Arrange immediate emergency medical assessment, since joint destruction can begin within days.

front: Where does acute hematogenous osteomyelitis most often start in children?
back: In the metaphysis of long bones such as the distal femur and proximal tibia. Signs include focal bone pain, fever, refusal to bear weight, and local tenderness.

front: A young child refuses to walk or sit, with low-grade fever and back pain. What diagnosis is suspected?
back: Discitis, an infection of the intervertebral disc. ESR and CRP are usually raised. Refer for imaging (MRI) and medical care rather than starting treatment.

front: How does transient synovitis of the hip differ from septic arthritis in a child?
back: Transient synovitis often follows a viral illness, with no or low fever, normal or mildly raised inflammatory markers, and the child can usually bear some weight. Septic arthritis does not fit this picture.

front: Which features of left arm, jaw, or chest pain suggest a cardiac source needing urgent referral?
back: Exertional onset relieved by rest, diaphoresis, nausea, dyspnea, and pain not changed by movement or palpation. If present at rest or severe, call 911 and do not continue treatment.

front: What is Kehr sign, and what does it suggest?
back: Acute left shoulder tip pain, referred from diaphragmatic irritation, most often from splenic rupture or intra-abdominal bleeding. Recent abdominal trauma makes it an emergency.

front: Right shoulder or scapular pain after a fatty meal, with nausea, suggests which organ source?
back: The gallbladder (cholecystitis or gallstones), referred through the phrenic nerve. The shoulder exam is typically normal and movement does not change symptoms. Refer for medical assessment.

front: An older male smoker has deep back pain and a pulsatile abdominal mass. What is suspected and what is done?
back: Abdominal aortic aneurysm. Pain that is constant and unaffected by movement raises concern. Do not palpate deeply, and arrange urgent or emergency medical care.

front: A client has unilateral calf swelling, warmth, and tenderness after surgery. What tool guides your decision?
back: The Wells score for deep vein thrombosis, based on risk factors and signs. Moderate or high probability needs same day medical referral for imaging. Do not massage the calf.

front: What are the four stages of fracture healing in order?
back: Inflammation (hematoma), soft callus, hard callus, then remodelling. Remodelling can take months to years, and loading is progressed according to the stage and stability.

front: What is the Salter-Harris SALTR mnemonic for pediatric growth plate fractures?
back: I Straight across the physis, II Above (through physis and metaphysis, most common), III beLow (epiphysis), IV Through (metaphysis, physis, epiphysis), V cRush. Higher types risk growth disturbance.

front: A fall on an outstretched hand causes anatomical snuffbox tenderness. What is the concern and management?
back: Scaphoid fracture, which risks avascular necrosis of the proximal pole due to retrograde blood supply. Immobilize and refer, because early radiographs may be negative.

front: Why is avascular necrosis a major risk after a displaced femoral neck fracture?
back: The femoral head blood supply runs retrograde from the medial femoral circumflex artery, which a displaced intracapsular fracture can disrupt. Watch for worsening groin pain and loss of function.

front: Which findings after a fracture suggest complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS)?
back: Pain out of proportion to the injury, allodynia, edema, skin colour and temperature change, sweating changes, and stiffness (Budapest criteria). Early recognition and referral improve outcomes.

front: Which patient factors commonly contribute to fracture nonunion?
back: Smoking, diabetes, poor nutrition, infection, inadequate immobilization or instability, and some medications such as long-term corticosteroids. Persistent pain at the site with no healing progression calls for medical review.

front: Which hip movements are restricted after total hip arthroplasty via the posterior approach?
back: Avoid flexion beyond 90 degrees, adduction past midline, and internal rotation. These positions risk posterior dislocation. Precautions follow the surgeon's protocol and duration.

front: Which combined movement is avoided after total hip arthroplasty via the anterior approach?
back: Hip extension combined with external rotation, which risks anterior dislocation. Posterior precautions are generally less strict, but the surgeon's protocol governs.

front: What is the general principle for early range of motion after rotator cuff repair?
back: Protect the repair: passive range first, with active elevation delayed until the surgeon clears it, often around 6 weeks. Timing varies with tear size and tissue quality.

front: Which deficit is typical after ACL reconstruction with a hamstring graft versus a patellar tendon graft?
back: Hamstring graft: hamstring weakness at the donor site. Patellar tendon graft: anterior knee pain and kneeling discomfort. Graft type shapes strengthening and monitoring.

front: Which postoperative findings after knee arthroplasty should prompt contact with the surgeon?
back: Increasing wound drainage, spreading redness, heat, fever, rising pain, or calf swelling. These suggest infection or thrombosis and need prompt medical assessment rather than progression of rehab.

front: What are the three stages of the tendinopathy continuum described by Cook and Purdam?
back: Reactive tendinopathy, tendon disrepair, and degenerative tendinopathy. Early stages respond to load reduction and gradual re-loading, while degenerative changes are less reversible.

front: How does the response to isometric loading help in a painful tendon?
back: Sustained isometric holds (for example 45 seconds) can temporarily reduce tendon pain, so they may be used to maintain loading when painful. The effect is short-term and varies.

front: How do a complete Achilles tendon rupture and Achilles tendinopathy differ at the bedside?
back: Rupture: sudden pop, palpable gap, weak plantarflexion, and positive Thompson test (no plantarflexion on calf squeeze). Tendinopathy: gradual, load-related localized pain and morning stiffness.

front: What does the arc sign suggest in midportion Achilles pain?
back: A swelling that moves with the tendon through ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion points to the tendon itself (midportion tendinopathy) rather than the paratenon or surrounding structures.

front: What does the Quebec Task Force classify, and what separates Grade II from Grade III?
back: Whiplash-associated disorder severity. Grade II is neck pain with musculoskeletal signs (reduced range, point tenderness). Grade III adds neurological signs. Grade IV is fracture or dislocation.

front: Which Canadian C-spine rule factors mandate radiography?
back: Age 65 or older, a dangerous mechanism (such as a fall from 1 m (5 stairs) or more, or axial load), or paresthesias in the extremities. Otherwise low-risk factors allow safe range assessment.

front: Which features help identify cervicogenic headache?
back: Unilateral side-locked pain starting in the neck, provoked by neck movement or sustained posture, reduced cervical range, and a positive flexion-rotation test for upper cervical dysfunction.

front: What headache features indicate an emergency referral rather than treatment?
back: A sudden thunderclap headache reaching peak intensity within a minute, or headache with fever and neck stiffness, neurological deficits, or after significant head trauma. Suspect hemorrhage or meningitis.

front: Why is the cervical spine examined in a client with concussion and persistent headache or dizziness?
back: Neck injury often coexists with concussion and can cause cervicogenic headache and dizziness. Identifying it directs treatment, while red flags still need medical clearance.

front: What does the FAST stroke recognition tool stand for, and what is the action step?
back: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call 911. Any one sign means a suspected stroke and an emergency, because clot-busting treatment and thrombectomy are time-dependent.

front: What is the scoring range of the NIHSS and what does a higher score indicate?
back: The National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale scores 0 to 42. A higher score means a more severe neurological deficit. It is used in acute stroke to grade severity and track change.

front: How does the Chedoke-McMaster Stroke Assessment describe motor recovery of the arm, leg, hand, and foot?
back: It uses a 7-stage scale per segment. Stage 1 is flaccid paralysis with no voluntary movement, and stage 7 is normal movement. Stages 2 to 3 reflect synergy and spasticity, which guide treatment choices.

front: Which line-bisection finding suggests hemineglect, and which lesion side is the classic cause?
back: The patient marks the line midpoint shifted toward the unaffected side and ignores the opposite half. Left-sided neglect after a right parietal stroke is most common. Star cancellation and clock drawing also screen for it.

front: On the Modified Ashworth Scale, what does grade 1+ describe?
back: A catch followed by minimal resistance through less than half of the range of motion. Grade 2 is a more marked increase through most of the range, but the part still moves easily.

front: What are the three Glasgow Coma Scale components, total range, and the severe injury cut-off?
back: Eye opening (1 to 4), verbal response (1 to 5), motor response (1 to 6). Total is 3 to 15. A score of 8 or less is severe, 9 to 12 moderate, and 13 to 15 mild.

front: At which Rancho Los Amigos level is a patient confused and agitated?
back: Level IV, confused and agitated. The patient is hyperactive, has a short attention span, and cannot learn new information. Management uses a calm, low-stimulation environment and avoids restraint where possible.

front: What defines post-traumatic amnesia, and when is it considered resolved?
back: PTA is the period after brain injury when the person cannot form continuous memories and is disoriented. It resolves when they are consistently oriented and recall daily events. Tools include the Westmead PTA Scale and GOAT.

front: What is the SCAT6, and what must a clinician remember about its use?
back: The Sport Concussion Assessment Tool, 6th edition, is for athletes aged 13 and older (Child SCAT6 is for ages 8 to 12). It supports assessment but cannot alone diagnose or exclude a concussion.

front: What is the sequence of return to learn and return to sport after a concussion in Canadian guidance?
back: Return to school or learning comes first, with gradual symptom-limited increases. A person should be back to full learning, with no symptoms, before progressing to full-contact sport and medical clearance.

front: What does an ISNCSCI AIS grade A (complete) injury mean?
back: No sensory or motor function preserved in the lowest sacral segments, S4 to S5. This includes no voluntary anal contraction and no deep anal pressure. Any sacral sparing makes the injury incomplete.

front: How does AIS grade C differ from AIS grade D?
back: Both are motor incomplete. In C, more than half of the key muscles below the neurological level are graded less than 3. In D, at least half of them are grade 3 or higher.

front: How is the neurological level of injury defined in ISNCSCI?
back: It is the most caudal segment with intact sensation and antigravity muscle strength (at least 3 of 5), provided the segments above are normal. Both sides are tested, and the single neurological level is the most cephalad (highest) of the sensory and motor levels.

front: Which key muscle represents C7 in the ISNCSCI motor examination?
back: Elbow extensors (triceps). Memory aid for the key muscles: C5 elbow flexors, C6 wrist extensors, C7 elbow extensors, C8 finger flexors, T1 finger abductors (small finger).

front: A patient with T4 spinal cord injury has a pounding headache and high blood pressure. What is the first action?
back: Suspect autonomic dysreflexia. Sit the person upright, loosen tight clothing, and look for a trigger such as bladder distension, catheter blockage, or bowel impaction. Call emergency services if it does not resolve.

front: What are the three Seddon grades of peripheral nerve injury?
back: Neurapraxia (conduction block, no axonal loss, recovers in days to weeks), axonotmesis (axon disrupted, endoneurium intact, regrowth about 1 mm per day), and neurotmesis (complete transection needing surgery).

front: How do Sunderland grades relate to Seddon's classification?
back: Sunderland has five grades. Grade 1 equals neurapraxia, grades 2 to 4 are progressively worse axonotmesis levels, and grade 5 is complete transection, equal to neurotmesis. Higher grades have poorer spontaneous recovery.

front: What arm posture is typical of an upper trunk (Erb) brachial plexus injury?
back: The waiter's tip position: shoulder adducted and internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated, wrist flexed. It comes from C5 and C6 damage, often with traction at birth or in a fall.

front: What is the classic presentation of Guillain-Barre syndrome and a key physiotherapy precaution?
back: Symmetric ascending weakness with areflexia, often after an infection. Monitor respiratory function and autonomic instability, and avoid overfatigue or intense strengthening, which can worsen weakness.

front: Which tool screens for loss of protective sensation in diabetic neuropathy of the foot?
back: The 10 g Semmes-Weinstein monofilament, applied at several plantar sites until it bends. Inability to feel it at one or more sites signals loss of protective sensation and higher ulcer risk.

front: What does Hoehn and Yahr stage 3 describe in Parkinson disease?
back: Bilateral disease with mild to moderate disability and postural instability, such as an abnormal pull test, but the person is still physically independent. Stage 2 is bilateral without balance impairment.

front: Which feature is required for a clinical diagnosis of parkinsonism, and what other signs accompany it?
back: Bradykinesia (slowness with decrement in amplitude or speed of repeated movement) plus rest tremor or rigidity. Postural instability usually appears later and is not required for diagnosis.

front: Name cueing strategies that help freezing of gait in Parkinson disease.
back: Visual cues such as lines or tape on the floor, auditory cues such as a metronome or counting, and attentional strategies such as stepping over an object or shifting weight before stepping.

front: What is festination in Parkinson disease?
back: Short, quickening steps with a forward-leaning trunk as the person chases their own centre of mass. It raises fall risk. Training uses larger deliberate steps, cueing, and turning in wide arcs.

front: Which tests and signs identify cerebellar ataxia on a physiotherapy exam?
back: Finger-to-nose with dysmetria and intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia on rapid alternating movements, heel-to-shin ataxia, and a wide-based gait. Unlike Parkinson tremor, cerebellar tremor worsens near the target.

front: How is a multiple sclerosis relapse defined for clinical purposes?
back: New or worsening neurological symptoms lasting at least 24 hours, without fever or infection, and occurring at least 30 days after the start of a previous relapse. Otherwise consider a pseudo-relapse.

front: What is Uhthoff phenomenon and how should a physiotherapist respond?
back: A temporary worsening of MS symptoms when core body temperature rises with heat, exercise, or fever. It is not a relapse. Cool the person, rest, and plan exercise with cooling strategies.

front: What principles guide management of fatigue in multiple sclerosis?
back: Fatigue is among the most common and disabling MS symptoms. Use pacing, energy conservation, scheduled rests, cooling, and regular moderate exercise. Avoid exercising to exhaustion, which can worsen next-day function.

front: What does an EDSS score of 6.0 mean in multiple sclerosis?
back: The Expanded Disability Status Scale runs 0 to 10. At 6.0 the person needs intermittent or unilateral constant assistance, such as a cane, to walk about 100 metres, with or without resting.

front: What is Lhermitte sign and which condition is it linked with?
back: An electric shock sensation running down the spine, sometimes into the limbs, on neck flexion. It points to dorsal cervical cord irritation and is classically associated with multiple sclerosis.

front: Which findings typify amyotrophic lateral sclerosis on examination?
back: A mix of upper motor neuron signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia) and lower motor neuron signs (atrophy, fasciculations), with sensation, eye movements, and bladder control typically preserved. Plan submaximal exercise and avoid fatigue.

front: What is Gowers sign and in which condition is it classic?
back: A child pushes up the thighs with the hands to rise from the floor because of proximal hip weakness. It is classic in Duchenne muscular dystrophy, an X-linked disorder with calf pseudohypertrophy.

front: How are GMFCS levels I and V described in cerebral palsy?
back: Level I walks without limitations, with reduced speed, balance, and coordination. Level V has very limited self-mobility and is transported in a manual wheelchair. Levels run I to V by age band.

front: Which spina bifida type is most severe, and which precaution applies to the care environment?
back: Myelomeningocele, where the spinal cord and meninges protrude, often with hydrocephalus and Chiari II malformation. Use latex-free equipment because of the elevated risk of latex allergy.

front: When do most children walk independently, and when is referral considered?
back: Most walk independently by about 12 to 15 months. Not walking by 18 months, or any loss of previously gained skills, warrants further assessment. Sitting without support is usually achieved by about 6 months.

front: What is the MoCA's maximum score, and which result is considered normal?
back: The Montreal Cognitive Assessment is scored out of 30, and 26 or higher is considered normal. One point is added if education is 12 years or fewer. It screens, but does not diagnose, cognitive impairment.

front: How does delirium differ from dementia in onset and attention?
back: Delirium has acute onset over hours to days, fluctuating course, and marked inattention. Dementia develops gradually with relatively preserved attention early on. Delirium is a medical emergency needing urgent referral.

front: Which features distinguish dementia with Lewy bodies from Alzheimer disease?
back: Lewy body dementia shows early visual hallucinations, fluctuating cognition, and parkinsonism with a falls risk. Alzheimer disease typically presents with early episodic memory loss that progresses gradually.

front: What does a score of 10 or more on the PHQ-9 suggest, and what item needs same-day action?
back: A score of 10 or higher suggests probable major depression, out of a possible 27. Any positive answer on item 9, thoughts of self-harm, needs same-day follow-up and referral per local policy.

front: What four abilities are considered when observing decision-making capacity?
back: Understanding relevant information, appreciating how it applies to oneself, reasoning about options, and expressing a choice. Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific, and adults are presumed capable unless shown otherwise.

front: When is a seizure treated as status epilepticus?
back: When it lasts longer than 5 minutes, or when seizures repeat without recovery of consciousness between them. It is a medical emergency, so call 911 and protect the airway and head.

front: What first aid steps apply during a generalized tonic-clonic seizure in the clinic?
back: Note the time, protect the head, clear the area, and loosen tight clothing. Do not restrain or put anything in the mouth. After jerking stops, turn the person onto their side.

front: How does an absence seizure differ from a focal impaired awareness seizure?
back: Absence seizures are brief staring spells of about 5 to 20 seconds with abrupt onset and recovery and no postictal state. Focal impaired awareness seizures last longer, often with automatisms and postictal confusion.

front: Which common triggers lower seizure threshold, and what is the exercise guidance?
back: Sleep deprivation, missed medication, alcohol, flashing lights, and hyperventilation. Regular exercise is generally safe and encouraged. Avoid hyperventilation and apply safety precautions around water, heights, and heat.

front: What is Todd paralysis?
back: Temporary focal weakness in a limb or side after a seizure, which usually resolves within about 48 hours. It must be distinguished from stroke, so any new or persistent deficit requires urgent medical assessment.

front: What is a positive Dix-Hallpike test for posterior canal BPPV?
back: After a few seconds of latency, vertigo with upbeating torsional nystagmus beats toward the undermost ear, lasting under 60 seconds and fatiguing on repeat. Treat with the Epley maneuver.

front: What does a corrective saccade on the head impulse test indicate?
back: Peripheral vestibular hypofunction on the side the head was turned toward, because the vestibulo-ocular reflex fails to hold gaze. A normal test in acute vertigo with nystagmus raises concern for a central cause.

front: What are the three HINTS components and which results suggest a central cause?
back: Head impulse, Nystagmus, Test of skew. Central signs are a normal head impulse, direction-changing or vertical nystagmus, and skew deviation. HINTS applies only in acute continuous vertigo with nystagmus.

front: How is the Dizziness Handicap Inventory scored and graded?
back: It has 25 items scored 0 to 100. Higher scores mean greater perceived handicap: 0 to 30 mild, 31 to 60 moderate, and 61 to 100 severe. It tracks the impact of dizziness over time.

front: How many items and what score range does the Berg Balance Scale have, and what score is commonly linked to higher fall risk?
back: It has 14 items scored 0 to 4 each, for a total of 56. Scores below 45 are commonly associated with increased fall risk in older adults, and lower scores mean worse balance.

front: What does the Timed Up and Go (TUG) test measure, and what time suggests increased fall risk in older adults?
back: It times standing from a chair, walking 3 metres, turning, returning and sitting. A time of 12 seconds or more (CDC STEADI cut-off) suggests increased fall risk; other studies cite 13.5 seconds.

front: In the 10-metre walk test, how is gait speed calculated and which part of the walkway is timed?
back: The client walks 10 metres, but only the middle 6 metres are timed, leaving 2 metres each end for acceleration and deceleration. Speed (m/s) equals 6 divided by the time in seconds.

front: What walking speeds separate household, limited community and full community ambulation (Perry classification)?
back: Below 0.4 m/s is household ambulation, 0.4 to 0.8 m/s is limited community ambulation, and above 0.8 m/s is community ambulation. Gait speed is a quick functional and prognostic marker.

front: What does the Mini-BESTest assess, and how is it scored?
back: It assesses dynamic balance across 14 items in four sections: anticipatory postural control, reactive postural control, sensory orientation and dynamic gait. Maximum score is 28, and it has fewer ceiling effects than the Berg.

front: What are the classic signs of bacterial meningitis, and how often are all three present together?
back: Fever, severe headache and neck stiffness (nuchal rigidity). Only a minority of patients show all three, so photophobia, vomiting or altered mental status with fever should also prompt urgent medical referral.

front: How are Kernig and Brudzinski signs elicited, and what do they suggest?
back: Kernig: with hip and knee flexed to 90 degrees, passive knee extension causes pain or resistance. Brudzinski: passive neck flexion causes hip and knee flexion. Both suggest meningeal irritation.

front: A feverish client has a non-blanching petechial rash and neck stiffness. What is the first action?
back: Treat as suspected meningococcal sepsis or meningitis: a medical emergency. Call emergency services (911) immediately and do not continue the physiotherapy session. Delay in antibiotics increases mortality.

front: What features separate encephalitis from meningitis?
back: Encephalitis involves brain parenchyma, so altered level of consciousness, personality change, seizures or focal deficits dominate, along with fever and headache. Herpes simplex virus is the most common sporadic viral cause.

front: What presentation suggests transverse myelitis, and why is it an urgent referral?
back: Rapid onset of bilateral weakness, a sensory level, and bladder or bowel dysfunction from spinal cord inflammation, often after infection. It needs urgent medical workup to protect cord function.

front: What is the normal resting heart rate range for adults?
back: 60 to 100 beats per minute. Below 60 is bradycardia and above 100 is tachycardia, though well-trained athletes may normally rest below 60. Always note rhythm regularity and symptoms.

front: What does a third heart sound (S3) suggest on cardiac auscultation?
back: An early diastolic ventricular gallop. In adults over about 40 it suggests volume overload and heart failure. It occurs from rapid ventricular filling of a dilated, stiff ventricle.

front: What are the Borg RPE scale range and the meaning of a rating of 13?
back: The original Borg RPE scale runs from 6 (no exertion) to 20 (maximal exertion). A rating of 13 means somewhat hard, roughly moderate intensity. Multiply a rating by 10 to estimate heart rate.

front: How does stable angina differ from pain of acute myocardial infarction?
back: Angina is brought on by exertion or stress and eases within minutes with rest or nitroglycerin. Infarction pain is usually more severe, lasts longer than 15 to 20 minutes, and is not relieved by rest. Treat as an emergency.

front: What do the four NYHA functional classes describe in heart failure?
back: Class I: no limitation. Class II: slight limitation, symptoms with ordinary activity. Class III: marked limitation, symptoms with less than ordinary activity. Class IV: symptoms at rest or with any activity.

front: What is the value of 1 MET?
back: 1 MET equals 3.5 mL of oxygen per kilogram per minute, the approximate resting oxygen consumption. Activities are expressed as multiples of this, for example brisk walking at about 3 to 4 METs.

front: During exercise testing, what blood pressure response is an absolute indication to stop?
back: A drop in systolic blood pressure of more than 10 mm Hg despite an increase in workload, when accompanied by other signs of ischemia. Also stop for worsening angina, severe dyspnea or dizziness.

front: How does the Canadian Cardiovascular Society classify heart failure by ejection fraction?
back: HFrEF: ejection fraction 40 percent or less. HF with mildly reduced EF: 41 to 49 percent. HFpEF: 50 percent or higher. The type guides medication choices and rehabilitation prescriptions.

front: Which clients are typically eligible for referral to cardiac rehabilitation?
back: Those after myocardial infarction, percutaneous coronary intervention or bypass surgery, plus stable chronic heart failure and valve surgery. Program entry is by referral, usually soon after the cardiac event.

front: How is the ankle-brachial index calculated, and what value suggests peripheral artery disease?
back: Highest ankle systolic pressure divided by highest brachial systolic pressure. Normal is 1.0 to 1.4. A value of 0.90 or lower indicates peripheral artery disease; above 1.4 suggests noncompressible vessels.

front: How does intermittent claudication typically present?
back: Reproducible calf, thigh or buttock cramping pain with walking, relieved within minutes of standing rest. It indicates arterial insufficiency, in contrast with neurogenic claudication, which eases with spinal flexion.

front: In the Wells score for DVT, what total indicates a likely DVT in the two-level model?
back: A score of 2 or more means DVT is likely; 1 or less means unlikely. Points are added for active cancer, calf swelling, pitting edema and others, and 2 are subtracted if another diagnosis is as likely.

front: What calf swelling difference scores a point in the Wells DVT criteria, and where is it measured?
back: Calf swelling of more than 3 cm compared with the asymptomatic leg, measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity. Pitting edema confined to the symptomatic leg is a separate criterion.

front: How do arterial and venous ulcers differ in location and appearance?
back: Arterial: painful, punched-out, pale base, on toes or pressure points, with cool, hairless skin. Venous: shallow, irregular, moist, near the medial malleolus (gaiter area), with edema and brown hemosiderin staining.

front: What hemoglobin levels define anemia in adults according to the WHO?
back: Below 130 g/L in men and below 120 g/L in non-pregnant women. Typical signs include fatigue, pallor, exertional dyspnea and tachycardia, which can limit exercise tolerance.

front: What is the normal platelet count, and what exercise precautions apply to a client with a low count?
back: Normal is 150 to 400 ×10⁹/L. With thrombocytopenia, avoid heavy resistance, deep massage and high-impact activity, watch for bruising and petechiae, and check recent counts with the medical team.

front: What triggers can precipitate a vaso-occlusive crisis in sickle cell disease?
back: Dehydration, cold exposure, hypoxia, infection and overexertion. Encourage hydration, warm environments and pacing; severe pain, chest pain or fever needs urgent medical care.

front: What does the INR monitor, and what is the usual therapeutic range for most warfarin indications?
back: INR monitors warfarin's effect on clotting. The usual target is 2.0 to 3.0. A higher INR raises bleeding risk, so check the latest value before manual therapy or vigorous exercise.

front: A client on an anticoagulant falls and reports a new severe headache. What is the first action?
back: Treat as possible intracranial bleeding: stop treatment and arrange emergency medical assessment. Anticoagulated clients can bleed internally after minor trauma, and signs may be delayed.

front: What do fine crackles on auscultation typically indicate, and when do they occur?
back: Crackles reflect the popping open of small airways or fluid and secretions in the airways. Fine, late-inspiratory crackles suggest interstitial lung disease or pulmonary edema; coarse crackles suggest secretions.

front: What does expiratory wheeze indicate, and how does it differ from stridor?
back: Wheeze is a high-pitched sound from narrowed intrathoracic airways, as in asthma or COPD. Stridor is a loud inspiratory sound from upper airway obstruction and is an emergency.

front: What are normal resting pulse oximetry values, and when can the reading be unreliable?
back: Normal SpO2 is about 95 to 100 percent. Readings can be unreliable with poor peripheral perfusion, cold fingers, nail polish, motion, or carbon monoxide poisoning, which falsely raises the value.

front: What is the modified Medical Research Council (mMRC) dyspnea scale?
back: A 0 to 4 scale of breathlessness with activity. Grade 0 is breathless only with strenuous exercise; grade 4 is too breathless to leave the house or when dressing. It is used in COPD.

front: What normal arterial pH and PaCO2 ranges are used, and what pattern is respiratory acidosis?
back: Normal pH is 7.35 to 7.45 and PaCO2 is 35 to 45 mm Hg (4.7 to 6.0 kPa). Respiratory acidosis is low pH with high PaCO2, from inadequate ventilation.

front: What spirometry finding confirms airflow obstruction in COPD?
back: A post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.70. This persistent, not fully reversible obstruction distinguishes COPD from restrictive disease, where the ratio is normal or high.

front: How does GOLD grade COPD severity by FEV1 percent predicted?
back: GOLD 1 (mild) is 80 percent or more, GOLD 2 (moderate) is 50 to 79, GOLD 3 (severe) is 30 to 49, and GOLD 4 (very severe) is below 30, in patients with FEV1/FVC below 0.70.

front: What bronchodilator response supports a diagnosis of asthma on spirometry?
back: An increase in FEV1 of at least 12 percent and 200 mL after bronchodilator indicates significant reversibility. Reversibility is typical of asthma but is usually limited in COPD.

front: What are the three cardinal symptoms of a COPD exacerbation?
back: Increased dyspnea, increased sputum volume and increased sputum purulence. Recognizing these in a client prompts medical review, and exercise should be paused until the exacerbation is managed.

front: What signs of a severe asthma attack require emergency care?
back: Inability to speak full sentences, accessory muscle use, cyanosis, exhaustion, confusion, or a silent chest with little air movement. A silent chest signals near-complete obstruction and is ominous.

front: What spirometry pattern defines restrictive lung disease?
back: Reduced FVC and total lung capacity with a normal or increased FEV1/FVC ratio, such as 0.80 or higher. Causes include interstitial lung disease, chest wall deformity and neuromuscular weakness.

front: How does a tension pneumothorax present, and what is the response?
back: Sudden severe dyspnea, tachycardia, hypotension, tracheal deviation away from the affected side, and absent breath sounds. It is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate 911 activation.

front: What chest findings are typical of a large pleural effusion?
back: Dullness to percussion, decreased or absent breath sounds, and reduced tactile fremitus over the fluid, sometimes with a pleural rub above it. Chest expansion is reduced on the affected side.

front: What findings on assessment suggest lobar pneumonia?
back: Fever, productive cough, pleuritic pain, crackles, bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion over the consolidated lobe. Increased tactile fremitus and egophony may also be present.

front: Which auscultation finding and symptoms suggest interstitial lung disease?
back: Fine, dry Velcro-like crackles at the lung bases, with progressive exertional dyspnea and a dry cough. Oxygen saturation often falls during exertion, so monitor SpO2 during exercise.

front: What gene and inheritance pattern cause cystic fibrosis?
back: Mutations in the CFTR gene on chromosome 7, inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. Defective chloride transport produces thick mucus, causing lung infection and pancreatic insufficiency.

front: What sweat chloride value supports a diagnosis of cystic fibrosis?
back: A sweat chloride of 60 mmol/L or higher is diagnostic. Values of 30 to 59 mmol/L are intermediate and need further testing, such as genetic analysis.

front: What is bronchiolitis and which virus most commonly causes it?
back: A viral lower respiratory infection of infants, usually under 2 years, most often from respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). It causes wheeze, crackles, feeding difficulty and increased work of breathing.

front: What are the hallmark signs of croup in a child?
back: A barking cough, hoarse voice and inspiratory stridor, usually from parainfluenza virus in children aged 6 months to 3 years. A steeple sign on neck X-ray is classic.

front: What signs during exercise should make a child with congenital heart disease stop?
back: Worsening cyanosis, dizziness, chest pain, syncope or unusual dyspnea. Children with cyanotic lesions or pulmonary hypertension tolerate exertion poorly, so follow cardiology exercise clearance.

front: What causes silicosis, and which workers are most at risk of developing it?
back: Inhaling respirable crystalline silica dust causes fibrotic lung nodules, usually in the upper lobes. At risk: miners, quarry and stone workers, sandblasters, tunnellers and foundry workers after years of exposure.

front: Which serious infection is people with silicosis at increased risk of developing?
back: Tuberculosis. Silica damages alveolar macrophages and weakens lung defences, so new cough, fever, night sweats or weight loss in a client with silicosis should prompt physician review and TB testing.

front: What precautions apply when a client has suspected or confirmed active pulmonary tuberculosis?
back: Airborne precautions: a negative-pressure single room, door closed, and a fit-tested N95 respirator for staff. The client wears a surgical mask when leaving the room. Defer non-urgent treatment until cleared.

front: What classic symptom cluster should make you suspect pulmonary tuberculosis?
back: Productive cough lasting more than 3 weeks, often with hemoptysis, plus fever, night sweats, fatigue and unintentional weight loss. Report to the physician and apply airborne precautions while it is investigated.

front: How should exercise be paced for a client with persistent post-COVID dyspnea and post-exertional symptom worsening?
back: Use symptom-guided pacing: start low, progress slowly, monitor SpO2, heart rate and symptoms, and avoid pushing through fatigue. Worsening 24 to 48 hours later signals the dose was too high.

front: How is a stage 1 pressure injury defined?
back: Intact skin with a localized area of non-blanchable erythema, which may look different on darker skin tones (purple or maroon discolouration). Check with fingertip pressure and look for warmth, firmness or pain.

front: What separates a stage 3 from a stage 4 pressure injury?
back: Stage 3 is full-thickness skin loss with visible fat but no exposed fascia, muscle, tendon, ligament, cartilage or bone. Stage 4 exposes fascia, muscle, tendon, ligament, cartilage or bone.

front: Using the adult rule of nines, what percentage of total body surface area is each leg (front and back)?
back: 18 percent per leg. Head 9, each arm 9, anterior trunk 18, posterior trunk 18, perineum 1. Used to estimate burn extent; the pediatric chart gives a larger head and smaller legs.

front: What does a healthy granulating wound bed look like?
back: Moist, bright red or beefy, bumpy tissue that bleeds easily. Pale or dusky granulation suggests poor perfusion or infection, and yellow slough or black eschar indicates non-viable tissue needing debridement.

front: How is stage 2 lymphedema described using the International Society of Lymphology staging?
back: Pitting becomes less evident and swelling does not reduce with limb elevation alone. Tissue fibrosis begins, so the limb feels firmer. Stage 1 is pitting edema that reduces with elevation.

front: What blood glucose level defines hypoglycemia in a person with diabetes according to Diabetes Canada, and how is it treated?
back: Below 4.0 mmol/L. If the client is alert, give 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate (such as juice or glucose tablets), recheck in 15 minutes, and repeat if it is still below 4.0.

front: What presentation suggests an acute Charcot foot in a client with diabetic neuropathy?
back: A warm, red, swollen foot, often with little pain, and skin temperature more than about 2 degrees C above the other foot. Offload immediately (usually a total contact cast) and refer urgently.

front: Which findings suggest hypothyroidism in a client presenting with fatigue and musculoskeletal complaints?
back: Cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, dry skin, bradycardia, slowed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes, and sometimes carpal tunnel syndrome or myalgia. Refer for thyroid function testing.

front: Which findings suggest hyperthyroidism rather than hypothyroidism?
back: Heat intolerance, weight loss despite good appetite, tachycardia or palpitations, fine tremor, anxiety and proximal muscle weakness. Check resting heart rate before exercise and refer if uncontrolled.

front: How are obesity classes defined by BMI in adults?
back: Class I is 30.0 to 34.9 kg/m2, class II is 35.0 to 39.9, and class III is 40 or higher. BMI is a screening measure and does not capture fat distribution or function.

front: What is diastasis recti, and how is it commonly assessed?
back: Widening of the linea alba between the rectus abdominis bellies. With the client in crook lying, lift the head slightly and palpate the gap above and below the umbilicus. More than about 2 cm is commonly considered wide.

front: How is the posterior pelvic pain provocation (P4 or thigh thrust) test performed, and what is positive?
back: Client supine with the hip flexed to 90 degrees; apply gentle downward force along the femur. Reproduction of familiar deep pain in the buttock or posterior pelvis is positive for pelvic girdle pain.

front: Why is placenta previa after 28 weeks an absolute contraindication to aerobic exercise in pregnancy?
back: Exercise and uterine activity raise the risk of bleeding from the low-lying placenta. Other absolute contraindications include ruptured membranes, premature labour, persistent unexplained bleeding, pre-eclampsia and an incompetent cervix.

front: Which findings suggest pre-eclampsia in a pregnant client?
back: New blood pressure of 140/90 mmHg or higher after 20 weeks with proteinuria or organ dysfunction. Symptoms include severe headache, visual disturbance, upper right abdominal pain and sudden facial or hand swelling. Refer urgently.

front: Which symptoms during prenatal exercise mean the client should stop and seek medical advice?
back: Vaginal bleeding, regular painful contractions, leaking fluid, dizziness or faintness, chest pain, severe headache, calf pain or swelling, and shortness of breath that does not settle with rest.

front: How does cancer-related fatigue differ from ordinary tiredness, and what is the main evidence-based treatment?
back: It is distressing, disproportionate to activity, and not relieved by rest. The strongest evidence supports regular aerobic and resistance exercise, with energy conservation and pacing adjusted to treatment cycles.

front: What does a Mirels score of 9 or higher indicate for a long bone metastasis?
back: High impending fracture risk, for which prophylactic fixation is generally recommended. The score uses site, pain, lesion type (lytic or blastic) and size. Avoid resisted or weight-bearing loading and contact the oncology team.

front: What absolute neutrophil count defines severe neutropenia?
back: Below 0.5 × 10⁹/L. Infection risk is very high, so use strict hand hygiene, clean equipment, avoid ill contacts and defer exercise in shared public spaces until the oncology team clears it.

front: What should you do if a client who is neutropenic has a temperature of 38.0 degrees C or higher?
back: Treat it as a medical emergency (febrile neutropenia). Stop treatment, do not start exercise, and arrange immediate medical assessment, because overwhelming sepsis can develop quickly.

front: How should a client with a fresh abdominal incision be taught to cough or sit up after surgery?
back: Splint the incision with a folded pillow or hands, and roll to the side to rise instead of sitting straight up. This reduces pain and strain on the wound while keeping airway clearance effective.

front: Does a client with HIV need special isolation precautions during physiotherapy?
back: No. Routine practices (standard precautions) apply to all clients, with hand hygiene, gloves for blood and body fluids, and sharps safety. HIV is not spread by casual contact or shared equipment.

front: Why is hepatitis B a higher occupational concern for physiotherapists than hepatitis C?
back: Hepatitis B is more infectious through blood and body fluid exposure, but a vaccine prevents it and health care workers should be immunized. There is no vaccine for hepatitis C.

front: Which hand hygiene method is required after contact with a client who has Clostridioides difficile infection?
back: Wash with soap and water, because alcohol-based hand rub does not reliably kill C. difficile spores. Use contact precautions with gown and gloves and clean equipment with a sporicidal agent.

front: What precautions apply when treating a client with MRSA infection or colonization?
back: Contact precautions: gown and gloves for direct care, hand hygiene, a dedicated or cleaned-between-clients set of equipment such as goniometers and plinths, and treating the client last or in a private space when possible.

front: Which features suggest systemic lupus erythematosus in a client with joint pain?
back: Malar (butterfly) rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, fatigue, non-erosive symmetrical arthritis, and serositis. Pace exercise around flares, advise sun protection, and monitor for steroid-related osteoporosis.

front: What does a score of 7 on the Clinical Frailty Scale mean?
back: Severely frail: completely dependent for personal care from any cause, physical or cognitive, but stable and not at high risk of dying within about 6 months. Scores run 1 (very fit) to 9 (terminally ill).

front: What are the three qSOFA criteria, and what does a positive screen mean?
back: Respiratory rate of 22 or more, altered mentation, and systolic blood pressure of 100 mmHg or less. Two or more suggests possible sepsis with a higher risk of poor outcome, so escalate urgently.

front: What MRC sum score indicates ICU-acquired weakness?
back: A sum score below 48 out of 60, from six muscle groups tested bilaterally (grade 0 to 5 each). The weakness is typically symmetrical, proximal and diffuse, in a client who was critically ill.

front: Why is polypharmacy important in a falls assessment, and which drug classes raise risk most?
