back: Taking five or more medications raises fall risk. Fall-risk-increasing drugs include benzodiazepines, other sedatives, antipsychotics, antidepressants, opioids and some antihypertensives. Ask for a pharmacist medication review.

front: Which features define delirium on the Confusion Assessment Method?
back: Acute onset with a fluctuating course, plus inattention, plus either disorganized thinking or an altered level of consciousness. Delirium is a medical emergency, and hypoactive forms are easy to miss.

front: What does a client who answers no to all seven general PAR-Q+ questions do next?
back: They can become more physically active without further screening, and sign the declaration. Any yes answer leads to the follow-up questions, which may require review by a qualified exercise professional or physician.

front: What do the Canadian 24-Hour Movement Guidelines recommend for adults aged 18 to 64 for physical activity?
back: At least 150 minutes of moderate to vigorous aerobic activity per week, muscle-strengthening activities at least 2 days per week, and several hours of light activity, as part of good sleep and less sedentary time.

front: What Timed Up and Go time suggests increased fall risk in a community-dwelling older adult?
back: 12 seconds or longer (the cut-off used in the CDC STEADI algorithm). Other cut-offs exist between studies, so interpret it with strength, balance and history rather than alone.

front: By what age is a child expected to walk independently, and when does it become a concern?
back: Most children walk independently between about 12 and 15 months. Not walking by 18 months, or any loss of previously gained skills, needs a pediatric developmental assessment or physician referral.

front: What rating on the Borg 6 to 20 scale corresponds to moderate exercise intensity?
back: About 12 to 14, described as somewhat hard. Each rating is roughly the heart rate divided by 10, so 13 equals about 130 beats per minute in a healthy adult, though medications change this.

front: Which non-drug strategies help relieve breathlessness at the end of life?
back: A handheld fan directed at the face, pursed-lip breathing, upright forward-leaning positions, a calm environment and pacing. Opioids are the usual drug option, prescribed by the physician.

front: What is the main aim of physiotherapy in palliative care?
back: To maintain function, comfort, dignity and independence for as long as possible according to the client's goals. Treatment goals shift as the condition advances, and care is shaped by goals-of-care discussions.

front: Why is a 30-degree side-lying tilt recommended for a bedbound client at high risk of pressure injury?
back: It keeps weight off the sacrum and the greater trochanter, which bear high pressure in a 90-degree side-lying position. Use pillows or wedges, and reposition on the schedule set by skin assessment.

front: Which tool do clinicians use to track symptom burden in palliative care, and what does it rate?
back: The Edmonton Symptom Assessment System rates pain, tiredness, drowsiness, nausea, lack of appetite, shortness of breath, depression, anxiety and well-being, each from 0 (none) to 10 (worst).

front: Which findings are red flags for cauda equina syndrome, and what is the action?
back: Saddle anesthesia, new urinary retention or incontinence, bowel dysfunction, sexual dysfunction and bilateral or progressive leg weakness. Send the client to emergency for urgent imaging and surgical review.

front: Which history and symptoms in a client with back pain raise suspicion of cancer?
back: Previous cancer, unexplained weight loss, age over 50, pain at night or at rest not relieved by position change, and failure to improve after one month. Refer to the physician for investigation.

front: Which calf finding in the Wells score for deep vein thrombosis is measured, and how?
back: Calf swelling of more than 3 cm compared with the other leg, measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity. Other items include unilateral pitting edema, localized tenderness and a recent immobilization or surgery.

front: What should you do if a client has chest pressure radiating to the jaw or left arm with sweating?
back: Stop activity, have the client rest, call 911 or the local emergency number, and monitor vital signs. Treat it as a possible acute coronary syndrome until a physician says otherwise.

front: What is the appropriate action if a client does not improve, or worsens, after a reasonable trial of treatment?
back: Reassess and reconsider the working diagnosis, screen again for red flags, and communicate with or refer to the physician or another provider. Continuing the same plan unchanged is not appropriate.

front: What does the PEACE part of the PEACE and LOVE acute soft tissue injury framework stand for?
back: Protect, Elevate, Avoid anti-inflammatories, Compress, Educate. It covers the first days after injury, when the focus is limiting excess movement and bleeding and teaching the patient about natural healing.

front: What does the LOVE part of the PEACE and LOVE framework stand for, and when does it apply?
back: Load, Optimism, Vascularization, Exercise. It applies after the first days: gradual pain-guided loading, a positive outlook, pain-free cardiovascular activity, then exercise to restore mobility, strength and proprioception.

front: How long should protection by rest typically last after an acute soft tissue injury?
back: Only about 1 to 3 days. Prolonged rest weakens tissue and slows recovery, so early pain-guided movement and loading should resume once the initial irritability settles.

front: What is the current evidence for ice as a treatment after acute soft tissue injury?
back: Evidence is limited. Ice may give short-term analgesia, but there is no strong proof it improves healing or function, and it may impair tissue repair. It should not be relied on as the main treatment.

front: Why does the PEACE framework advise avoiding anti-inflammatory medication in the early phase of a soft tissue injury?
back: Inflammation is part of normal tissue repair. Anti-inflammatories may blunt it and impair long-term healing of muscle, tendon and ligament, so the framework recommends avoiding them early.

front: In the Maitland grading system, what do grades I and II describe?
back: Small amplitude (grade I) and large amplitude (grade II) oscillations performed in the early to mid range, before tissue resistance. They are mainly used to reduce pain and modulate irritability.

front: In the Maitland grading system, what do grades III and IV describe?
back: Grade III is a large amplitude oscillation into resistance, grade IV a small amplitude oscillation at the end of range. They are used to stretch stiffness and restore joint mobility.

front: What is a grade V mobilization (manipulation)?
back: A small amplitude, high velocity thrust at the end of the available range. An audible cavitation may occur, but it is not required for a clinical effect.

front: Name four absolute contraindications to spinal manipulation.
back: Fracture, spinal cord compression or cauda equina syndrome, suspected cervical artery dysfunction, and spinal infection or malignancy. A positive finding on screening means no thrust technique, and the patient needs medical referral.

front: Before cervical manipulation, which structure's dysfunction must the physiotherapist screen for, and why?
back: The cervical arteries (vertebral and carotid). Neck pain and headache can be early signs of arterial dissection, and manipulation could worsen it, so a risk screen following the IFOMPT framework is required.

front: What do the letters in FITT stand for in exercise prescription?
back: Frequency, Intensity, Time (duration), Type. These four variables define the exercise dose, and each can be adjusted to progress or regress a program.

front: What principle states that the body adapts specifically to the demands placed on it?
back: Specificity (the SAID principle: specific adaptation to imposed demands). Training should match the task, such as muscle group, movement pattern, contraction type and speed that the patient needs to improve.

front: What is progressive overload?
back: Gradually increasing training demand, such as load, repetitions, sets or complexity, above what the tissue is used to. Without it, strength and fitness gains plateau.

front: Why do beginners gain strength quickly in the first few weeks of resistance training?
back: Early gains are mostly neural: better motor unit recruitment and coordination. Visible muscle hypertrophy follows later, usually after about 6 to 8 weeks of consistent training.

front: What is the CSEP recommendation for adults aged 18 to 64 for aerobic activity?
back: At least 150 minutes per week of moderate to vigorous aerobic activity, accumulated in bouts of any length, plus muscle strengthening activities using major muscle groups at least 2 days per week.

front: How does motor control training differ from strength training in dosage?
back: Motor control training uses low loads, high attention to movement quality, precise feedback and repetition of correct patterns. Strength training uses high loads near the muscle's capacity to drive tissue adaptation.

front: What does the STarT Back screening tool do in low back pain management?
back: It stratifies patients into low, medium and high risk of persistent disability using physical and psychosocial items (yellow flags), so treatment intensity can be matched to risk.

front: What is the core advice for a patient with acute nonspecific low back pain?
back: Reassure them, explain that the prognosis is good, advise them to stay active and return to normal activities as pain allows, and avoid prolonged bed rest. Routine imaging is not needed without red flags.

front: What is the usual natural course of acute nonspecific low back pain?
back: Most episodes improve substantially within about 6 weeks, though recurrence is common. Pain lasting beyond 12 weeks is classified as chronic.

front: What is meant by centralization in directional preference assessment?
back: With repeated movements in a direction, referred leg or buttock pain moves proximally toward the spine. It is a favourable prognostic sign and suggests that direction of movement may guide exercise.

front: What does a yellow flag indicate in low back pain?
back: A psychosocial risk factor for persistent disability, such as fear avoidance beliefs, catastrophizing, depression, or low job satisfaction. Yellow flags call for education, graded activity and sometimes multidisciplinary care.

front: What approach to return to work is recommended for a worker recovering from low back pain?
back: Early, graded return with modified duties or hours rather than waiting for full pain resolution. Work participation supports recovery and reduces the risk of long-term disability.

front: Which exercise type is a core component of guideline-based care for mechanical neck pain?
back: Neck and scapulothoracic strengthening plus deep cervical flexor and craniocervical control training. Exercise is supported by stronger evidence than passive modalities for neck pain.

front: What advice do guidelines give about cervical collars after whiplash injury?
back: Avoid prolonged collar use. Early advice to stay active and perform gentle neck movement leads to better recovery than immobilization, unless a fracture or instability has been identified.

front: In the Quebec Task Force classification of whiplash associated disorders, what is grade II?
back: Neck complaint with musculoskeletal signs such as decreased range of motion and point tenderness, without neurological signs. Grade III adds neurological signs, and grade IV is fracture or dislocation.

front: Which three muscles form the scapular upward rotation force couple?
back: Upper trapezius, lower trapezius and serratus anterior. Weakness or poor timing of these muscles, especially serratus anterior, alters scapular position and can contribute to shoulder pain.

front: Which exercises are commonly used to strengthen serratus anterior in shoulder rehabilitation?
back: Push-up plus and wall slides or punches with scapular protraction. They train protraction and upward rotation with relatively low activation of upper trapezius.

front: What is the usual first-line approach for rotator cuff related shoulder pain?
back: Education plus a progressive exercise program of rotator cuff and scapular strengthening, with load adjusted to pain. Trials show exercise gives results similar to surgery for many patients with subacromial pain.

front: After a rotator cuff repair, what is the typical early rehabilitation phase?
back: Sling protection with passive range of motion only, avoiding active contraction of the repaired tendon. Active motion and strengthening begin later, with timing set by the surgeon's protocol and repair size.

front: What are the three classic stages of adhesive capsulitis?
back: Freezing (painful, progressive stiffness), frozen (stiff, pain easing) and thawing (gradual return of motion). Treatment is matched to irritability: pain control early, mobility work later.

front: Which hip movements are restricted by posterolateral approach total hip arthroplasty precautions?
back: Hip flexion beyond 90 degrees, adduction past midline, and internal rotation. Combining them puts the new joint at risk of posterior dislocation. Precaution duration depends on the surgeon.

front: Which movement combination is the dislocation risk after an anterior approach total hip arthroplasty?
back: Extension combined with external rotation. Precautions after an anterior approach therefore avoid these movements, in contrast to the flexion, adduction and internal rotation limits of a posterior approach.

front: When should mobilization usually begin after total joint arthroplasty?
back: On the day of surgery or the first postoperative day. Early mobilization lowers the risk of blood clots and pneumonia and shortens hospital stay.

front: What is the stair technique with crutches or a cane after lower limb surgery?
back: Up with the good, down with the bad. The unaffected leg leads when climbing, and the affected leg and the aid lead when descending.

front: What does weight bearing as tolerated (WBAT) mean?
back: The patient may put as much weight through the limb as pain allows, guided by their symptoms. It differs from partial, touch-down and non-weight bearing, which set specific limits.

front: What are common early goals after total knee arthroplasty?
back: Full knee extension, flexion of about 90 degrees within the first weeks, quadriceps activation, edema control and independent walking with an aid. Lack of extension predicts a poor gait outcome.

front: What is the limb symmetry index (LSI) used in return to sport testing?
back: Involved limb performance divided by uninvolved limb performance, multiplied by 100. Many protocols require at least 90 percent on strength and hop tests before an athlete returns to pivoting sport.

front: Name the common hop tests used to assess readiness after ACL reconstruction.
back: Single hop for distance, triple hop for distance, crossover hop for distance and 6 metre timed hop. Together they assess power, control and symmetry between limbs.

front: Why is return to pivoting sport before about 9 months after ACL reconstruction discouraged?
back: Research shows reinjury risk falls as return is delayed until at least 9 months, and when strength and hop criteria are met. Early return carries a markedly higher risk of graft rupture.

front: Which early goal is the priority after ACL reconstruction?
back: Restoring full knee extension and controlling effusion, along with quadriceps activation. Loss of extension early can lead to persistent gait problems and anterior knee pain.

front: How does rehabilitation after meniscal repair differ from partial meniscectomy?
back: Repair protects the healing tissue, with limited weight bearing and limits on deep flexion early on. Partial meniscectomy allows quicker weight bearing and progression as symptoms settle.

front: Which ligament is most commonly injured in a lateral ankle sprain?
back: The anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL), usually from an inversion and plantar flexion mechanism. The calcaneofibular ligament is the next most often involved.

front: What is the preferred management of an acute grade I or II lateral ankle sprain?
back: Functional treatment: a brace or tape for support, early weight bearing and progressive exercise. This gives a faster return to activity than prolonged immobilization.

front: What type of training best reduces recurrence of lateral ankle sprains?
back: Balance and proprioceptive training, and continued use of a brace or tape for sport. Neuromuscular control exercise lowers the rate of repeat sprains.

front: What is the Alfredson protocol for midportion Achilles tendinopathy?
back: Eccentric heel drops with straight and bent knee, 3 sets of 15, twice daily, 7 days a week for 12 weeks. Pain during the exercise is allowed within tolerance.

front: What is the classic presentation of plantar fasciopathy?
back: Heel pain with the first steps in the morning or after rest, tender over the medial calcaneal origin. A positive windlass test supports the diagnosis. High load calf and foot strengthening helps.

front: What isometric dose is often used for pain relief in tendinopathy?
back: About 5 holds of 45 seconds at roughly 70 percent of maximal voluntary contraction. It can reduce pain short term and allows loading to start in painful, irritable tendons.

front: What is heavy slow resistance (HSR) training for tendinopathy?
back: Heavy loading performed slowly, about 3 seconds up and 3 seconds down, with load increasing as repetitions drop over roughly 12 weeks. It gives results comparable to eccentric training and is better tolerated.

front: In a pain monitoring model for tendinopathy, what pain level is generally acceptable during loading?
back: Up to about 5 out of 10, provided it settles by the next morning and does not worsen over 24 hours. Higher pain or lasting morning stiffness means the load should be reduced.

front: What are the four stages of secondary (indirect) fracture healing, in order?
back: Inflammation (hematoma), soft callus (cartilage), hard callus (woven bone), then remodelling. Loading and activity are progressed to match the stage, because early stress on soft callus can disrupt union.

front: Name common client factors that delay fracture healing and need to be addressed in the care plan.
back: Smoking, diabetes, poor nutrition, infection, poor blood supply, NSAID or corticosteroid use, and excessive motion at the fracture site. Counselling on smoking cessation and nutrition supports union.

front: What does weight bearing as tolerated (WBAT) mean after a lower limb fracture?
back: The client may load the limb as far as pain allows, from partial up to full weight, unless the surgeon states a limit. Use a gait aid and monitor pain and swelling.

front: Which findings after a distal radius fracture should raise suspicion of complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS)?
back: Pain out of proportion to the injury, allodynia, swelling, skin colour and temperature change, sweating change, and stiffness. Diagnosis uses the Budapest criteria. Early movement, edema control, and desensitization help prevention.

front: After casting, which pain pattern suggests acute compartment syndrome rather than normal fracture pain?
back: Pain out of proportion to the injury, worsened by passive stretch of the muscles in the compartment, with tense swelling. It is a surgical emergency, so arrange urgent medical assessment.

front: How is osteoporosis defined by bone mineral density using the WHO T-score?
back: A T-score of minus 2.5 or lower at the hip or spine on DXA scan. Osteopenia (low bone mass) is between minus 1.0 and minus 2.5. A fragility fracture can also establish the diagnosis.

front: Which spinal movements should a client with osteoporosis and vertebral compression fracture risk avoid?
back: Loaded forward flexion and combined flexion with twisting, such as sit-ups or toe touches with weights. Teach hip hinging, neutral spine, and extension-based posture and back strengthening instead.

front: What exercise program components are recommended to maintain bone health in adults with osteoporosis?
back: Progressive resistance training, weight-bearing impact activity as tolerated, balance training, and posture work. Skeletal loading must be progressive and individualized, with fracture history and pain guiding the intensity.

front: Which type of exercise is most effective in preventing falls in older adults living in the community?
back: Balance and strength training that is progressively challenging and done regularly, such as the Otago Exercise Programme. Add a home hazard review, footwear check, and medication review.

front: What does the FRAX tool estimate, and how is it used in osteoporosis management?
back: It estimates the 10-year probability of a major osteoporotic fracture and hip fracture from clinical risk factors, with or without bone density. It helps identify clients who need treatment and referral.

front: What are the first-line core treatments for knee and hip osteoarthritis?
back: Education, exercise (strengthening and aerobic), and weight management for those who are overweight. These come before medication or surgery and should be offered to every client with symptomatic osteoarthritis.

front: What is the GLA:D program, and what does it include?
back: Good Life with osteoArthritis in Denmark: patient education plus supervised neuromuscular exercise for hip and knee osteoarthritis, typically two education sessions and twelve exercise sessions over six weeks, with a home program.

front: How much does losing 1 kg of body weight reduce knee joint load with each step in walking?
back: About 4 kg of compressive load per step. This is why weight loss counselling is a core part of knee osteoarthritis care, along with exercise and activity pacing.

front: In which hand should a client with right hip osteoarthritis hold a cane, and why?
back: The left hand, opposite the painful hip. The cane and the right leg move together, and the cane's lever arm reduces the hip abductor force and joint load.

front: What advice is given for managing a flare-up of osteoarthritis pain?
back: Temporarily reduce load and modify activity, keep gentle movement going, use heat or cold for comfort, and return to the usual exercise program gradually. A written flare plan builds self-management confidence.

front: List joint protection principles taught to clients with rheumatoid arthritis.
back: Use larger, stronger joints, avoid prolonged static positions and tight gripping, respect pain, distribute load over several joints, and use assistive devices and ergonomic tools to lower stress on inflamed joints.

front: How does morning stiffness duration help differentiate rheumatoid arthritis from osteoarthritis?
back: Rheumatoid arthritis causes morning stiffness lasting longer than about 60 minutes, while osteoarthritis stiffness usually settles within 30 minutes. Prolonged stiffness suggests inflammatory disease and needs medical referral.

front: What exercise emphasis is recommended for a client with ankylosing spondylitis?
back: Daily spinal extension and mobility exercises, chest expansion and deep breathing, posture training, and aerobic activity. Stiffness improves with movement, not rest, which differs from mechanical back pain.

front: What is the usual long-term serum urate target in gout management, and what is the physiotherapist's education role?
back: Below 360 micromol/L, achieved with urate-lowering medication prescribed by the physician. The physiotherapist educates on adherence, flare management (rest the joint), weight, alcohol reduction, and gradual return to activity.

front: What is activity pacing for a client with inflammatory arthritis?
back: Balancing activity and rest through planned breaks, spreading tasks over the day, and reducing activity during flares. It prevents the cycle of overdoing on good days followed by painful days.

front: What are the typical parameters for conventional (high-frequency) TENS for pain relief?
back: Frequency about 80 to 120 Hz, short pulse duration (about 50 to 200 microseconds), comfortable sensory-level intensity without muscle contraction. It works mainly through the gate control mechanism and can be used for long periods.

front: How does acupuncture-like (low-frequency) TENS differ from conventional TENS?
back: Frequency is low, about 2 to 4 Hz, with longer pulses and a strong intensity that produces visible muscle twitching. It acts through endogenous opioid release, so onset is slower but relief lasts longer.

front: Which situations are contraindications or precautions for applying TENS?
back: Demand-type cardiac pacemaker, over the anterior neck or carotid sinus, over the pregnant uterus, broken or infected skin, and areas of impaired sensation. Never place electrodes across the chest in cardiac clients without medical clearance.

front: Over which areas should therapeutic ultrasound not be applied?
back: Over malignancy, the pregnant uterus, the eyes, and areas of impaired sensation or circulation. Avoid over metal implants with heat-producing modes, and keep the sound head moving to prevent hot spots.

front: How does interferential current (IFC) work, and why is it used?
back: Two medium-frequency currents (about 4000 Hz) cross to produce a low-frequency beat inside the tissue. Medium frequency lowers skin resistance, so deeper tissue is stimulated with more comfort. It is used for pain and edema.

front: Which conditions are contraindications to superficial heat application?
back: Acute inflammation or fresh trauma, impaired sensation, poor arterial circulation, active bleeding, malignancy over the area, and deep vein thrombosis. Heat increases blood flow and metabolism, which worsens these conditions.

front: Which client conditions are precautions or contraindications for cryotherapy?
back: Cold urticaria, Raynaud's phenomenon, cryoglobulinemia, impaired sensation, peripheral vascular disease, and open wounds with poor circulation. Check the client's skin response early in the first application.

front: What is the typical duration for applying an ice pack, and how is the skin protected?
back: About 10 to 20 minutes with a damp or dry towel barrier between the ice and the skin. Check skin colour and sensation before, during, and after to prevent a cold burn.

front: How is a contrast bath usually performed for a swollen hand or foot?
back: Alternate warm water (about 3 to 4 minutes) with cold water (about 1 minute), repeating several cycles and finishing with cold when edema is the goal. Avoid in impaired sensation or vascular disease.

front: Which properties of water make aquatic exercise useful for clients with painful weight-bearing joints?
back: Buoyancy unloads joints and allows movement with less pain, hydrostatic pressure helps reduce edema, and water resistance strengthens muscles. Open wounds, uncontrolled incontinence, and infection are contraindications.

front: How is the correct height of a cane or walker set for an adult?
back: The handle sits at the level of the greater trochanter or wrist crease when standing, giving about 20 to 30 degrees of elbow flexion when gripped. Too high or low causes poor posture and shoulder strain.

front: How are crutches fitted to avoid nerve injury under the arm?
back: Crutch pads sit about two to three finger widths (about 5 cm) below the axilla. Weight goes through the hands and not the armpit, because pressure on the axilla can cause radial nerve (crutch) palsy.

front: Which gait pattern with crutches is used for a client who must stay non-weight-bearing on one leg?
back: Three-point gait: both crutches and the unaffected leg bear weight, while the affected leg is held off the ground. Swing-to and swing-through patterns are options with good balance and upper body strength.

front: What is the rule for climbing and descending stairs with crutches or a cane?
back: Up with the good leg first, down with the affected leg and the aid first. The memory hook is: up with the good, down with the bad. Always guard from behind going up and in front going down.

front: When is a four-point gait pattern with two crutches chosen?
back: For clients with poor balance, weakness in both legs, or ataxia, who need a slow, stable pattern that keeps three points of contact on the ground at all times. It is slower than three-point or swing gait.

front: What is the main indication for an ankle-foot orthosis (AFO) in gait rehabilitation?
back: Foot drop from dorsiflexor weakness, such as after stroke or peroneal nerve injury. The AFO holds the ankle near neutral so the toes clear the floor in swing phase and heel strike is safer.

front: How is a new orthosis introduced into daily use?
back: Use a graded wearing schedule, adding time gradually, and check skin after each period. Redness that does not fade within about 20 to 30 minutes of removal signals excess pressure and needs adjustment.

front: What are the usual phases of rehabilitation for a person after lower limb amputation?
back: Preoperative, acute postoperative, pre-prosthetic, prosthetic fitting and training, and community reintegration with long-term follow-up. Each phase has goals for wound healing, limb shaping, strength, and function.

front: How is a residual limb wrapped with an elastic bandage to control edema and shape it?
back: Use diagonal or figure-of-eight turns from distal to proximal, with the most pressure distally and decreasing proximally, and cover the joint above. Avoid circular wraps that create a tourniquet effect.

front: Which positions should a person with a transfemoral amputation avoid to prevent hip contracture?
back: Prolonged hip flexion, abduction, and external rotation, such as a pillow under the residual limb or long sitting. Teach lying prone and hip extension exercises to maintain range.

front: What is the core message of pain neuroscience education for a client with chronic pain?
back: Pain is a protective output of the nervous system and does not always equal tissue damage. In persistent pain the system becomes sensitized, so hurt does not mean harm, which reduces fear and supports movement.

front: What is graded exposure in the management of chronic pain with fear-avoidance?
back: Building a hierarchy of feared or avoided activities and gradually doing them, beginning with the least threatening, to reduce fear and improve function. Progress is time-based and does not depend on pain levels.

front: What is the difference between activity pacing and boom-bust behaviour in chronic pain?
back: Pacing sets activity quotas by time and gradually increases them regardless of pain on that day. Boom-bust is overdoing on good days, then resting for days after a flare, which maintains deconditioning and pain.

front: What are yellow flags in the assessment of a client with persistent pain?
back: Psychosocial risk factors for chronicity, such as catastrophizing, fear-avoidance beliefs, low mood, poor coping, and job dissatisfaction. They guide the care plan toward education, behaviour change, and interdisciplinary referral.

front: By the IASP definition, after how long is pain considered chronic?
back: When it persists or recurs for longer than three months. Chronic primary pain is a condition in its own right, while chronic secondary pain arises from another disease or injury.

front: How do stress urinary incontinence and urge urinary incontinence differ?
back: Stress incontinence is leakage with effort such as coughing, sneezing, or lifting, due to weak sphincter and pelvic floor support. Urge incontinence is leakage with a sudden strong need to void, linked to bladder overactivity.

front: What is the first-line physiotherapy treatment for stress urinary incontinence in women?
back: Supervised pelvic floor muscle training, with proper contraction technique confirmed (squeeze and lift), then progressive strength and endurance holds plus a trained 'knack' contraction before coughing or lifting.

front: What does bladder training involve for overactive bladder?
back: Scheduled voiding with gradually lengthened intervals toward a goal of about 3 to 4 hours, plus urge suppression using pelvic floor contractions and relaxation. A bladder diary tracks fluid intake, voiding, and leaks.

front: What is the role of biofeedback in pelvic floor rehabilitation?
back: It gives visual or auditory feedback of pelvic floor muscle activity from EMG or ultrasound, helping the client learn correct contraction and relaxation, especially when she cannot feel or isolate the muscles.

front: What conservative measures are used for symptomatic mild to moderate pelvic organ prolapse?
back: Pelvic floor muscle training, constipation management, avoiding heavy lifting and straining, weight management, and a vaginal pessary when appropriate. Surgical referral is considered when conservative care fails.

front: Which muscle is shortened in congenital muscular torticollis, and what head posture results?
back: The sternocleidomastoid is shortened or fibrotic. The head tilts toward the affected side while the chin rotates toward the opposite side. Early stretching and positioning give the best outcomes.

front: What is the purpose of a Pavlik harness, and what position error must be avoided?
back: It holds the infant hip flexed and abducted in a safe zone to keep the femoral head centred in developmental hip dysplasia. Forced or excessive abduction risks avascular necrosis of the femoral head.

front: What Cobb angle defines scoliosis on a standing radiograph?
back: A lateral curve with a Cobb angle of 10 degrees or more, with vertebral rotation. Smaller curves are called asymmetry. Cobb angle is the standard measure for tracking progression.

front: In which adolescent scoliosis curves is bracing typically considered?
back: Skeletally immature adolescents with curves of about 25 to 40 degrees and remaining growth. The goal is to prevent progression, not to correct the curve. Larger curves are referred for surgical opinion.

front: A child has tenderness over a growth plate and a normal radiograph. How should it be managed?
back: Treat as a Salter-Harris type I physeal fracture until proven otherwise: protect, immobilize, and refer. Missed growth plate injury can cause growth arrest or angular deformity.

front: What does the acronym SMART stand for in goal setting?
back: Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound. A goal such as walking 500 metres without a cane in four weeks meets all five criteria and can be checked at reassessment.

front: Name the components of the ICF framework used to organize physiotherapy goals.
back: Body functions and structures, activities, and participation, shaped by environmental and personal contextual factors. Goals at activity and participation levels reflect what matters most to the patient.

front: How is goal attainment scaling scored?
back: Each goal is rated from minus 2 to plus 2. Zero is the expected outcome, minus values are less than expected, and plus values are better than expected. It allows individualized goals to be compared.

front: Which factors guide how often and how long a patient needs physiotherapy?
back: Tissue healing stage, severity and irritability, patient function and goals, comorbidities, self-management ability, and access or funding. Dosing is reassessed as the patient responds.

front: Why write goals at the activity and participation level rather than as impairments only?
back: They describe what the patient wants to do, such as climbing stairs at home, and can be measured by performance. Impairment gains like range of motion do not guarantee functional change.

front: How is a Grade II hamstring strain defined?
back: A partial tear of muscle fibres with noticeable loss of strength, bruising, and pain with activity. Grade I is minor fibre damage, and Grade III is a complete rupture.

front: Which exercise type is emphasized in hamstring strain rehabilitation and prevention?
back: Eccentric hamstring strengthening, such as the Nordic hamstring exercise, progressed gradually. It improves load tolerance of the muscle-tendon unit and lowers recurrence risk in sport.

front: What is myositis ossificans and what early treatment should be avoided?
back: Heterotopic bone forming within muscle after a contusion, commonly the quadriceps. Avoid early deep massage, heat, and aggressive passive stretching, which can provoke further bleeding and ossification.

front: What does criteria-based return to play mean?
back: The athlete progresses by meeting objective criteria such as pain-free movement, strength symmetry, and sport-specific function tests, not by elapsed time alone. It lowers the risk of premature return.

front: What does the POLICE principle for acute soft tissue injury stand for?
back: POLICE (protection, optimal loading, ice, compression, elevation) is an older framework that has been superseded by PEACE and LOVE, because evidence for ice and routine compression is weak. Its useful idea was optimal loading in place of complete rest, since controlled early movement supports tissue healing.

front: What splint position is used for conservative management of carpal tunnel syndrome?
back: A night wrist splint holding the wrist in neutral. Flexed or extended wrist positions raise carpal tunnel pressure, so neutral keeps pressure on the median nerve lowest during sleep.

front: Which skin areas are affected in carpal tunnel syndrome, and which are spared?
back: Palmar thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger are affected. The thenar eminence skin is spared because the palmar cutaneous branch leaves the median nerve before the tunnel.

front: What is the purpose of tendon gliding exercises after hand surgery or injury?
back: They promote independent gliding of the flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus tendons to limit adhesions. The sequence moves through straight, hook, full fist, tabletop, and straight fist positions.

front: What is the first-line approach to hand edema control?
back: Elevate the hand above heart level with active finger and wrist movement, and add compression or retrograde massage as appropriate. Persistent edema leads to stiffness and adhesions.

front: What is the intrinsic-plus (safe) hand position used in splinting?
back: Wrist slightly extended, MCP joints flexed about 70 to 90 degrees, and IP joints extended. It keeps collateral ligaments lengthened and prevents contracture of the MCP and IP joints.

front: What is the purpose of a functional capacity evaluation?
back: To objectively measure what a person can safely do physically, compared with job demands, to guide return-to-work decisions. Results depend on consistent effort and use standardized, reliable tests.

front: What does a job demands analysis document?
back: The physical, cognitive, and environmental requirements of a job, such as lifting loads, postures, repetition, and pace. It gives a target for rehabilitation and for matching worker to tasks.

front: What is the principle of graded return to work?
back: Hours and duties are increased in steps, often with modified tasks, coordinated with the employer and worker. It builds tolerance, supports confidence, and lowers the risk of re-injury.

front: In the hierarchy of controls, which workplace ergonomic measures come first?
back: Eliminate the hazard or use engineering controls, such as an adjustable workstation or lift aid, before administrative controls and personal protective equipment. Higher controls protect all workers, not just one.

front: What does the duty to accommodate require of Canadian employers?
back: Under human rights legislation, employers must adapt work for an injured worker's needs up to the point of undue hardship. Physiotherapists provide restrictions and abilities, not just a diagnosis.

front: What do neuromuscular injury prevention programs like FIFA 11+ include, and what do they reduce?
back: Running warm-up, strength, balance, and plyometric exercises with landing technique. Used consistently as a warm-up, they reduce lower-limb injuries such as ACL and ankle sprains in team sport athletes.

front: Why does load management matter in injury prevention?
back: Sudden spikes in training load relative to what the athlete is accustomed to raise injury risk. Gradual progression of volume and intensity lets tissues adapt and keeps chronic load high.

front: What is the immediate action for an athlete with a suspected concussion?
back: Remove from play immediately, assess, and do not return to sport that day. Red flags such as worsening headache, repeated vomiting, or confusion need urgent medical assessment.

front: How does stepwise return to sport after concussion progress?
back: Each step lasts at least 24 hours, moving from symptom-limited activity to aerobic exercise, sport drills, non-contact training, then full practice. If symptoms return, go back to the previous step.

front: In the Canadian Guideline on Concussion in Sport, what order is followed for school and sport?
back: Return to school comes before return to sport. A student should manage a full school day without symptom worsening before starting contact sport, and medical clearance is needed for full contact.

front: What is a practical strategy to improve home exercise program adherence?
back: Prescribe a few key exercises, give written or video instructions, tie them to an existing daily routine, and agree on a plan with the patient. Long, complex programs reduce adherence.

front: What does OARS stand for in motivational interviewing?
back: Open questions, affirmations, reflective listening, and summarizing. These skills draw out the patient's own reasons for change and support autonomy rather than telling them what to do.

front: What is self-efficacy and how can a physiotherapist build it?
back: Confidence in one's ability to carry out a behaviour. It grows through mastery experiences: start with achievable exercises, progress gradually, and give feedback on success.

front: Name the stages of the transtheoretical model of behaviour change.
back: Precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, and maintenance. Matching advice to the stage works better than giving action plans to someone who is not yet ready to change.

front: What should a self-management plan for a chronic musculoskeletal condition include?
back: Core exercises, activity pacing, a flare-up plan, and clear signs of when to seek help. It lets the patient manage symptoms independently and lowers reliance on repeated treatment visits.

front: What must be obtained and documented before dry needling?
back: Informed consent covering the procedure, benefits, and risks such as bruising, pain, and rare pneumothorax. The patient must be able to decline or stop at any time, and the discussion is documented.

front: How is dry needling regulated in Canadian physiotherapy practice?
back: Authorization and training requirements vary by province and regulatory college. A physiotherapist may perform it only if their college permits it and they hold the required competence.

front: Name a contraindication to dry needling at a site.
back: Local skin infection, or patient refusal. Bleeding disorders, anticoagulant use, and lymphedema in the limb need extra caution or avoidance. Needle phobia also limits use.

front: What does the evidence say about kinesiology taping for musculoskeletal pain?
back: Trials show small or no clinically important benefit over sham taping. Tape may still be used as an adjunct for proprioceptive cueing, with skin checked for adhesive allergy or irritation.

front: When is soft tissue mobilization contraindicated over an area?
back: Over a suspected deep vein thrombosis, open wounds, skin infection, or known malignancy at the site. These carry risk of embolism, spread of infection, or tumour disruption.

front: How does water immersion level affect weight bearing in aquatic therapy?
back: Buoyancy unloads the joints. Standing at chest level, the body bears only about 25 to 35 percent of its weight (about 50 percent at waist level, about 10 percent at neck level). Shallower water gives more loading, so depth is chosen for the weight-bearing goal.

front: Why is caution needed with aquatic therapy in patients with heart failure?
back: Hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid toward the chest and increases venous return and cardiac preload. This can overload a failing heart, so such patients need medical clearance and monitoring.

front: Name situations in which pool therapy should be avoided.
back: Open wounds, active infection, uncontrolled seizures, and fecal incontinence. These risk infection spread or safety problems in the water, so they are standard precautions to screen.

front: Why is perceived exertion preferred for monitoring aerobic exercise in water?
back: Heart rate responses are lower during immersion than on land at the same effort. Rating of perceived exertion gives a more reliable measure of intensity than target heart rate alone.

front: What do CSEP guidelines recommend for adult physical activity weekly?
back: At least 150 minutes of moderate to vigorous aerobic activity per week, plus muscle strengthening on at least two days. Patients with musculoskeletal conditions work toward this gradually.

front: What are common criteria for discharging a patient from musculoskeletal physiotherapy?
back: Goals are met, progress has plateaued, the patient can self-manage, or the patient chooses to stop. Reasons and outcomes are documented, and referral is considered if goals remain unmet.

front: What should a maintenance program at discharge include?
back: A written exercise program with a plan for progression, guidance on activity levels, and advice on how often to continue. It protects gains and supports long-term self-management.

front: What is a relapse plan in discharge planning?
back: A set of steps the patient follows if symptoms flare, including self-care actions, warning signs, and when to book a return visit or seek medical care. It reduces fear and delays in seeking help.

front: Give an example of a community program for transition after discharge for knee or hip osteoarthritis.
back: GLA:D Canada, an education and exercise program delivered by trained physiotherapists. Community programs support continued activity, social support, and long-term management after formal care ends.

front: What belongs in a discharge summary for musculoskeletal care?
back: Outcome measures compared with baseline, goals achieved, remaining problems, and recommendations. It is shared with the referral source or other providers with the patient's consent.

front: What are the key features of task-specific training after stroke, and why is it favoured over general exercise?
back: Practise the actual functional task (reaching, sit to stand, walking) with many repetitions and progressive challenge. Neuroplasticity is specific, so gains transfer best to the task trained.

front: What motor criterion is usually required before offering constraint-induced movement therapy to a client after stroke?
back: Some residual voluntary movement in the affected hand, typically about 20 degrees of active wrist extension and 10 degrees of finger extension. The unaffected hand is restrained during much of the waking day while the affected arm trains intensively.

front: How should a physiotherapist handle a hemiplegic shoulder to reduce the risk of subluxation and pain?
back: Support the arm during transfers and positioning, handle the scapula and trunk rather than pulling on the arm, and avoid overhead pulleys. Traction on a flaccid shoulder stretches the capsule and promotes pain.

front: What is the role of body weight supported treadmill training in stroke gait rehabilitation?
back: It permits high repetition stepping practice with safe harness support for clients who cannot yet walk well overground. Support is reduced and speed is increased as the client improves, to build walking speed and endurance.

front: What is a sound positioning principle in bed for a client with hemiplegia after stroke?
back: Alternate positions, including side lying on the affected side with the arm forward and scapula protracted. Avoid prolonged supine lying, which promotes extensor tone and shoulder retraction, and give regular position changes to protect skin.

front: In motor learning, what is the difference between knowledge of results and knowledge of performance?
back: Knowledge of results is feedback about the outcome of the movement (did the cup reach the target). Knowledge of performance is feedback about movement pattern or quality (trunk leaned forward during the reach).

front: Which practice schedule favours long-term retention and transfer: blocked or random practice?
back: Random (variable) practice. Blocked practice (one task repeated) gives better performance during early acquisition, but random practice produces better retention and transfer, so progress from blocked to random as the client improves.

front: Why is giving feedback after every single attempt not ideal when teaching a motor skill?
back: Constant feedback can create dependence and weaken retention when it is withdrawn. Reduced or faded feedback frequency, with summary feedback after several trials, encourages the learner to use their own error detection.

front: When is whole-task practice preferred over part-task practice in motor learning?
back: Whole practice suits simple or highly integrated tasks whose parts depend on each other, such as gait. Part practice suits complex, serial tasks with separable components, and should be reintegrated into the whole task soon after.

front: Name the principles of experience-dependent neuroplasticity that guide intensity and dosage in neurological rehabilitation.
back: Use it or lose it, use it and improve it, specificity, repetition matters, intensity matters, salience (task must be meaningful), and timing matters. High repetition and challenge drive cortical reorganization.

front: What is the usual sequence of return to activity after a sport concussion in Canadian guidelines?
back: Relative rest, symptom-limited activity, light aerobic exercise, sport-specific exercise, non-contact drills, then full practice after medical clearance, then game play. Progress only if symptoms have not worsened at the current stage, usually for at least 24 hours before moving to the next stage.

front: How should a physiotherapist manage a client with traumatic brain injury who is agitated and confused (Rancho Los Amigos level IV)?
back: Reduce stimulation: quiet room, short sessions, familiar staff, one simple instruction at a time, and no restraint of movement where avoidable. Keep the environment safe rather than correcting or arguing.

front: What does the Buffalo Concussion Treadmill Test determine, and how is it used in rehabilitation?
back: It finds the heart rate at which symptoms are first provoked. Subthreshold aerobic exercise, typically about 80 percent of that heart rate, is then prescribed to promote recovery without worsening symptoms.

front: Which cognitive strategies help a client with memory impairment after traumatic brain injury during therapy?
back: Use errorless learning, chunking of tasks, consistent routines, repetition, and external aids such as notebooks, calendars and phone alarms. Giving one-step commands reduces cognitive load and error.

front: What Glasgow Coma Scale scores define mild, moderate and severe traumatic brain injury?
back: Mild is 13 to 15, moderate is 9 to 12, and severe is 8 or less. The scale scores eye opening, verbal response and motor response, with a total range of 3 to 15.

front: What is the first action for a client with spinal cord injury at T6 or above who develops autonomic dysreflexia?
back: Sit the client upright, lower the legs, loosen tight clothing or binders, and check the bladder and bowel for the trigger, such as a kinked catheter. Monitor blood pressure and call emergency help if it persists.

front: How often should a wheelchair user with spinal cord injury perform pressure relief, and why?
back: Typically every 15 to 30 minutes, held for 1 to 2 minutes, by push-up, forward lean or side lean. This restores blood flow over the ischial tuberosities and prevents pressure injuries.

front: Which muscle is key for independent level transfers in a client with a C7 spinal cord injury?
back: The triceps, which stabilizes the elbow in extension so the arms can depress the body. Sliding board transfers are used when full lifting is not possible, and shoulder preservation must be taught.

front: Why do clients with cervical spinal cord injury need an assisted cough, and how is it performed?
back: Paralyzed abdominal muscles cannot generate cough force. The clinician applies a timed upward abdominal thrust as the client exhales, below the rib cage, to help clear secretions and prevent pneumonia.

front: How does moving the rear axle of a manual wheelchair forward affect the chair?
back: It makes propulsion easier and the chair more manoeuvrable, but it reduces rearward stability and increases tipping risk. Anti-tip devices are often used while the client learns the balance point.

front: Why are external cues effective for freezing of gait in Parkinson disease?
back: The basal ganglia are impaired in generating automatic, internally timed movement. Visual cues (floor lines) or auditory cues (metronome, rhythmic counting) shift control to intact, attention-based cortical pathways.

front: What is the standard dosage of LSVT BIG for Parkinson disease?
back: Four consecutive weeks of one-hour sessions, four days per week, with daily home practice. It trains large-amplitude whole-body movement to counter bradykinesia and hypokinesia.

front: When should a physiotherapist schedule a session for a client with Parkinson disease relative to levodopa dosing?
back: During the medication peak, the "on" period, typically about one hour after a dose. Mobility is best and the client can engage in more intense training with less risk.

front: At which Hoehn and Yahr stage does postural instability first appear in Parkinson disease?
back: Stage 3, with impaired righting reflexes and bilateral involvement, while the client is still physically independent. Balance training and fall prevention become a priority at this point.

front: What aerobic exercise target is recommended for people with Parkinson disease?
back: Moderate to vigorous aerobic exercise, working toward 150 minutes per week, plus strength and balance training. Exercise improves mobility, and treadmill walking can be progressed in speed and incline.

front: What is Uhthoff phenomenon in multiple sclerosis, and how is it managed in rehabilitation?
back: A temporary worsening of symptoms with rising body temperature that resolves with cooling. Use cool environments, cooling vests, cold drinks and pre-cooling before exercise, and avoid hot baths or overheating.

front: What are the four Ps of energy conservation taught for MS fatigue?
back: Pace, plan, prioritize and position. Spread tasks through the day, schedule demanding activity when energy is highest, drop low-value tasks, and use efficient posture and seated work.

front: What exercise guidelines exist for adults with mild to moderate MS disability?
back: Aerobic exercise at least twice weekly for 30 minutes at moderate intensity, plus strength training of major muscle groups at least twice weekly. These Canadian MS guidelines improve fitness and function.

front: How should exercise be structured to avoid triggering excessive fatigue in a client with MS?
back: Use short bouts with rest breaks, moderate intensity, a cool setting, and the time of day with least fatigue, often morning. Avoid exercising to exhaustion and monitor symptoms over the next day.

front: How does a pseudo-exacerbation differ from a true relapse in MS?
back: A pseudo-exacerbation is a temporary worsening of symptoms from heat, infection or stress that resolves within 24 hours. A true relapse involves new or worsening neurological symptoms lasting longer than 24 hours.

front: What respiratory measures (the 20, 30, 40 rule) suggest impending respiratory failure in Guillain-Barre syndrome?
back: Vital capacity below 20 mL/kg, maximal inspiratory pressure weaker than minus 30 cmH2O, and maximal expiratory pressure below 40 cmH2O. Such values prompt consideration of ventilatory support.

front: What exercise approach is recommended for a client in the recovery phase of Guillain-Barre syndrome?
back: Gentle, low-intensity, submaximal exercise with frequent rests. Overwork fatigue can set back recovery, so avoid fatiguing resistance training and watch for autonomic instability such as blood pressure swings.

front: What exercise precaution applies to a client with ALS?
back: Use submaximal, low-resistance exercise and avoid overwork weakness. Stop or reduce the program if fatigue or weakness persists into the next day. Range of motion and stretching help limit contractures.

front: When is non-invasive ventilation usually considered in ALS?
back: When forced vital capacity falls to about 50 percent of predicted or sooner, or with symptoms of nocturnal hypoventilation, such as morning headache. Mechanical cough assist is added when cough strength declines.

front: What foot care advice should a physiotherapist give to a client with diabetic peripheral neuropathy?
back: Inspect feet daily, wear well-fitting protective footwear, never walk barefoot, and check bath water with a thermometer or the elbow. Loss of sensation allows unnoticed injury and ulceration.

front: Which orthosis and equipment are typically planned for foot drop and progressive weakness in neuromuscular disease?
back: An ankle-foot orthosis for foot drop, a collar for head drop in ALS, and early power wheelchair assessment as the disease progresses. Anticipating equipment avoids delay when function declines.

front: What does a GMFCS level III child with cerebral palsy typically use for mobility?
back: A hand-held mobility device such as a walker indoors, and wheeled mobility for longer distances. Level I walks without limitation, level II walks with limitations on uneven surfaces, IV needs powered mobility, V is transported.

front: Why is the GMFCS used when setting goals for children with cerebral palsy?
back: It classifies self-initiated movement, sitting and mobility by age band into five levels, and predicts likely motor development. Goals and equipment are matched to the child's level rather than to typical development.

front: Which children with cerebral palsy have the highest risk of hip displacement, and what measure is used to monitor it?
back: Children at GMFCS levels IV and V. Hip surveillance with radiographs measures the Reimers migration percentage, where a value above 30 percent is concerning and prompts orthopedic referral.

front: How does a solid ankle-foot orthosis differ from a hinged one in a child with cerebral palsy?
back: A solid AFO blocks ankle plantar flexion and dorsiflexion to control equinus and stabilize stance. A hinged AFO allows dorsiflexion for sit to stand and stairs while still limiting plantar flexion.

front: What is family-centred care in pediatric neurological rehabilitation?
back: Parents and the child are partners who set goals and share decisions. Tools such as the Canadian Occupational Performance Measure and Goal Attainment Scaling capture the family's own priorities.

front: Which canal and finding does the Epley maneuver treat?
back: Posterior canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, confirmed by a positive Dix-Hallpike test with upbeating torsional nystagmus. The head is moved through positions to move otoconia out of the canal.

front: What are the Brandt-Daroff exercises and who uses them?
back: A home habituation exercise for positional vertigo: the client sits, lies quickly on one side with the head turned about 45 degrees up, waits until vertigo settles, returns upright, and then alternates sides.

front: How is the VOR x1 viewing gaze stabilization exercise performed?
back: The client fixes the eyes on a stationary target while turning the head horizontally or vertically at a speed that keeps the target clear. It is used for unilateral vestibular hypofunction and progressed with speed and background.

front: What is the principle of habituation exercises in vestibular rehabilitation?
back: Repeated, controlled exposure to a movement that provokes dizziness reduces the response over time. It suits motion-provoked dizziness and is graded to symptom tolerance.

front: Which nystagmus findings suggest a central rather than peripheral cause and should prompt referral?
back: Purely vertical or downbeating nystagmus, nystagmus without latency that does not fatigue, or new neurological signs. Peripheral BPPV nystagmus has a short latency, fatigues, and is torsional.

front: What are the main features of the Otago Exercise Programme for falls prevention?
back: An individualized, progressive program of leg strengthening and balance exercises delivered by a physiotherapist, usually at home, three times weekly, plus walking. It targets adults aged 65 and older, especially those over 80.

front: Why is tai chi recommended in falls prevention programs for older adults?
back: Slow controlled weight shifting and postural control practice challenge balance, and trials show it reduces falls. It is suitable as a group program in the community.

front: What dose of balance exercise is linked with greater fall reduction in older adults?
back: At least 3 hours per week of challenging balance exercise, ideally combined with strength training. Multicomponent programs that progress difficulty are more effective than walking alone.

front: Who benefits most from home hazard modification, and what changes are made?
back: Older adults at high risk, particularly those with prior falls, with an occupational therapist assessing. Typical changes are removing loose rugs, adding grab bars and lighting, and securing nonslip surfaces.

front: What does the Modified Ashworth Scale measure, and what does a grade of 3 indicate?
back: It grades muscle tone (resistance to passive movement) from 0 to 4. Grade 3 means considerable increase in tone, with passive movement difficult throughout the range of motion.

front: Why is a prolonged low-load stretch preferred over a quick, forceful stretch for a spastic muscle?
back: A quick stretch triggers the stretch reflex and increases tone. Slow, sustained, low-load stretching reduces reflex activation and gives a better chance of lengthening the muscle and maintaining joint range.

front: What is the purpose of serial casting in a client with a developing plantarflexion contracture?
back: Serial casting applies a sustained, low-load stretch. The cast is changed repeatedly, each time positioning the joint nearer the end of range, to gradually lengthen soft tissue and regain dorsiflexion.

front: Which skin and circulation checks are essential when applying a resting hand or ankle splint to a spastic limb?
back: Check for redness that does not fade within about 20 to 30 minutes, pressure over bony prominences, swelling, and circulation or sensation changes. Establish a wearing schedule and teach the client or caregiver to inspect skin.

front: A client with spasticity is started on botulinum toxin injections. What is the physiotherapist's role?
back: Collaborate with the prescribing physician: identify target muscles, then time stretching, strengthening, splinting and task practice during the weeks of effect. Reassess tone and function to judge outcome.

front: When is an intermittent pneumatic compression pump contraindicated for a swollen leg?
back: Avoid it with suspected or confirmed acute deep vein thrombosis, uncontrolled heart failure, active infection such as cellulitis, or severe arterial insufficiency, since it may dislodge a clot or overload circulation.

front: What communication approach helps when a client with moderate dementia becomes agitated during a session?
back: Stay calm, use a low tone, short simple one-step cues, and approach from the front at eye level. Do not argue or correct. Validate feelings and redirect to a familiar task.

front: What is one benefit of regular exercise for older adults with dementia?
back: Exercise can improve physical function, mobility and balance, and may improve mood and sleep. It reduces fall risk when it includes balance and strength components and is practised consistently.

front: How should a physiotherapist teach a new exercise to a client with dementia who has impaired short-term memory?
back: Rely on procedural memory: use demonstration, repetition and consistent routine, same time and place. Give single-step cues and avoid depending on written or verbal recall of instructions.

front: Why is caregiver involvement important in a home program for a client with dementia?
back: The client may not remember or start exercises independently. Trained caregivers can cue, supervise safety, keep routine consistent, and report changes. Include caregiver education and respite needs in the plan.

front: Which types of exercise can help clients with mild to moderate depression, and what should the plan include?
back: Aerobic exercise, and resistance training, both show benefit for mild to moderate depression. Plan regular sessions, graded progression and social contact, and coordinate with the client's mental health team.

front: What are the typical phases of cardiac rehabilitation?
back: Phase I is inpatient, early mobilization. Phase II is a supervised outpatient program with monitoring. Phase III is long-term maintenance with independent, community or home-based exercise and risk factor management.

front: How is the target heart rate calculated using the heart rate reserve (Karvonen) method?
back: Target HR = resting HR + (percentage intensity x (maximal HR minus resting HR)). It individualizes intensity using the reserve, and is common when no stress test with a measured maximum is available.

front: On the Borg 6 to 20 rating of perceived exertion scale, what range is usually targeted for moderate cardiac exercise?
back: About 11 to 14, corresponding to light to somewhat hard effort. RPE is useful when heart rate response is blunted, for example in clients taking beta-blockers.

front: Why is heart rate an unreliable intensity guide for a client taking beta-blockers?
back: Beta-blockers blunt the heart rate response to exercise, so target heart rates from age-based formulas overestimate the rate. Use RPE, the talk test, and a heart rate target set from the client's own stress test.

front: Name two signs during cardiac rehab exercise that should prompt stopping the session.
back: Chest pain or angina, severe shortness of breath, dizziness, a drop in systolic blood pressure with increasing workload, pallor, or new arrhythmia. Stop, rest and follow the facility emergency plan.

front: What energy conservation strategies help a client with heart failure manage daily activities?
back: Pace tasks with planned rest breaks, sit for activities such as grooming, prioritize essential tasks, spread effort across the day, and avoid tasks right after meals or in extreme heat or cold.

front: Why should a client with heart failure be taught to weigh themselves daily?
back: Rapid weight gain (commonly more than 2 kg in 2 to 3 days) signals fluid retention. The client should report it early so treatment can be adjusted before hospitalization.

front: Which findings suggest worsening fluid overload in a client with heart failure?
back: Increasing edema, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, rapid weight gain, crackles on auscultation and increased fatigue or breathlessness at lower activity levels. Report them to the medical team.

front: What shoulder precaution is commonly given soon after pacemaker implantation?
back: Avoid raising the arm on the implant side above shoulder height and avoid heavy lifting, vigorous or forceful arm movements for the period advised by the surgeon, to protect lead position while it settles.

front: How should exercise intensity be set for a client with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD)?
back: Keep peak heart rate at least 10 to 20 beats per minute below the programmed ICD shock threshold, and confirm the threshold with the cardiology team before progressing the exercise program.

front: What is the main aim of supervised walking therapy for intermittent claudication?
back: Walk to moderate claudication pain, rest until it settles, then repeat, for sessions of 30 to 60 minutes at least three times a week. It improves pain-free and maximal walking distance.

front: A client has a calf-pain presentation with warmth, swelling and a high Wells score. What is the first action?
back: Suspect deep vein thrombosis: do not massage or vigorously exercise the leg, avoid further mobilization until it is assessed, and refer urgently for diagnostic imaging and medical management.

front: What is the major contraindication to compression therapy for leg edema or venous ulcers?
back: Significant arterial disease, usually judged by an ankle-brachial index below about 0.5, with only reduced compression under specialist guidance between 0.5 and 0.8. Compression may reduce already limited arterial blood flow and cause tissue damage.

front: What essential foot care advice should be given to a client with diabetes and peripheral arterial disease?
back: Inspect feet daily, wear well-fitting protective footwear, never walk barefoot, keep skin moisturized but dry between toes, and report any wound, blister or colour change promptly.

front: What are the three phases of the active cycle of breathing technique (ACBT)?
back: Breathing control, thoracic expansion exercises (deep breaths with an optional hold), and the forced expiration technique (huffs). Cycles repeat, with breathing control between to prevent bronchospasm and fatigue.

front: Which positions are used for postural drainage of the right middle lobe?
back: Lie on the left side, rotated about a quarter turn backward, with the foot of the bed raised about 15 degrees (Trendelenburg). Modify or avoid head-down positions with reflux, cardiac instability or raised intracranial pressure.

front: Name two situations where head-down postural drainage positions should be avoided or modified.
back: Uncontrolled hypertension, heart failure with orthopnea, gastroesophageal reflux, raised intracranial pressure, recent eye or neurosurgery, or hemoptysis. Use modified or flat positions and monitor tolerance.

front: How does a positive expiratory pressure (PEP) device assist secretion clearance?
back: Breathing out against resistance creates back pressure that splints airways open, preventing early collapse and moving secretions toward larger airways, where huffing or coughing can clear them.

front: What should the physiotherapist do before using high-frequency chest wall oscillation on a client?
back: Screen for contraindications such as unstable head or neck injury, recent chest trauma or surgery, untreated pneumothorax, hemoptysis or rib fractures, then fit the vest correctly and monitor comfort and oxygen saturation.

front: Why is a huff preferred over a forceful cough for clients with airway collapse, such as COPD?
back: A huff keeps the glottis open and generates lower pleural pressure, so airways collapse less. It moves secretions with less fatigue and less bronchospasm than repeated forceful coughing.

front: How does pursed-lip breathing help clients with COPD?
back: Exhaling against pursed lips creates back pressure that keeps small airways open longer, reducing air trapping and respiratory rate. It lowers breathlessness during exertion and recovery.

front: What is the typical oxygen saturation goal during exercise for clients with COPD who need supplemental oxygen?
back: Titrate oxygen to keep SpO2 at or above about 88 to 92 percent during exertion, per the prescribing guideline, and stop and rest or adjust flow if saturation falls below the target.

front: What exercise intensity is recommended for aerobic training in pulmonary rehabilitation?
back: Start with moderate intensity, often 60 to 80 percent of peak work rate or a Borg dyspnea rating of 3 to 4 out of 10, and progress as tolerated. Include both lower and upper limb training.

front: Which energy conservation strategy applies when a client with COPD climbs stairs?
back: Pace the climb by coordinating breathing with steps, for example inhaling at rest and exhaling through pursed lips while climbing, and pause on landings. Plan rest instead of rushing.

front: Why does early mobilization after major abdominal surgery reduce pulmonary complications?
back: Upright posture and walking increase lung volumes, improve ventilation and secretion clearance, and prevent atelectasis and pneumonia. Pain control and supported coughing, such as splinting the incision, help.

front: How should a client use an incentive spirometer correctly?
back: Exhale fully, seal lips around the mouthpiece, inhale slowly and deeply to raise the indicator, hold the breath for about 3 to 5 seconds, then exhale. Repeat about 10 times each hour while awake.

front: What is atelectasis, and what is a key sign on examination?
back: Collapse of alveoli causing loss of lung volume. Expect diminished breath sounds, possible bronchial breathing, reduced chest expansion over the area and increased work of breathing or low oxygen saturation.

front: A mechanically ventilated ICU client is being considered for mobilization. What is one safety criterion to check?
back: Check hemodynamic and respiratory stability: for example, stable blood pressure and heart rate, adequate oxygenation, no uncontrolled arrhythmia, no raised intracranial pressure, and an alert enough client who can follow commands.

front: Which physiological change from prolonged bed rest in the ICU prompts early progressive mobility?
back: Rapid loss of muscle mass and strength (ICU-acquired weakness), along with deconditioning and reduced lung volumes. Early mobility improves function and may shorten delirium and hospital stay.

front: What is exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB)?
back: Transient narrowing of the airways during or soon after vigorous exercise, causing cough, wheeze, chest tightness or breathlessness. It is triggered by dry, cool air and is relieved or prevented by bronchodilators.

front: When should a client with asthma use a short-acting bronchodilator before exercise?
back: Typically 10 to 15 minutes before exercise, if prescribed. A gradual warm-up can also reduce symptoms. Keep the reliever inhaler available throughout the session.

front: What should the physiotherapist do if a client with asthma develops wheeze and tightness during exercise?
back: Stop activity, have the client sit upright and use the reliever inhaler as prescribed, and monitor. If symptoms do not settle or worsen, follow the emergency plan and seek urgent medical help.

front: Why is airway clearance a daily therapy in cystic fibrosis?
back: Thick, sticky mucus causes airway obstruction, chronic infection and inflammation. Daily clearance with techniques such as ACBT, PEP, oscillating devices or vest therapy slows lung damage.

front: What should the physiotherapist remind clients with cystic fibrosis about hydration and salt during exercise?
back: They lose extra sodium in sweat, so they need adequate fluids and added salt to avoid dehydration and heat illness, especially in hot weather or long sessions.

front: What blood pressure level defines hypertension in the current Hypertension Canada guideline?
back: The 2025 Hypertension Canada guideline defines hypertension as BP of 130/80 mmHg or higher measured with a validated device under optimal conditions, confirmed with out-of-office measurement. The treatment target is systolic below 130 mmHg if tolerated. Drug therapy is recommended at 140/90 or higher, or at systolic 130-139 with high cardiovascular risk.

front: Above what resting blood pressure should a physiotherapist generally defer vigorous exercise testing or training?
back: A resting systolic above about 180 mmHg or diastolic above about 110 mmHg is a common reason to delay or cancel exercise. Refer for medical review and follow the facility policy for the client.

front: What breathing precaution applies when a client with hypertension performs resistance exercises?
back: Avoid the Valsalva maneuver. Breathing out during the effort and in during the return lowers the spike in blood pressure and reduces intrathoracic pressure surges.

front: What exercise recommendation do Canadian guidelines give to adults with hypertension for aerobic training?
back: Accumulate 150 minutes per week of moderate intensity aerobic activity, in sessions of at least 10 minutes. Regular exercise lowers blood pressure and cardiovascular risk.

front: Which blood pressure response during exercise should prompt stopping?
back: A fall in systolic pressure of more than 10 mmHg with increasing workload, or a systolic above about 250 mmHg or diastolic above 115 mmHg. Stop, rest and monitor, and report to the physician.

front: What is the usual therapeutic INR target for most warfarin indications, and why does it matter before exercise planning?
back: The usual target is 2.0 to 3.0. A supratherapeutic INR raises bleeding risk, so confirm the recent value with the care team before resistance or balance training and hold high-risk activity if it is elevated.

front: A client on a DOAC or warfarin has fall risk. Name three safety planning steps for physiotherapy sessions.
back: Clear the environment, use gait aids and supervision during balance work, avoid high-impact or contact activity, and teach the client to report any fall, head strike, or unusual bruising promptly, since bleeding can be delayed.

front: Which bleeding signs should a client on anticoagulants be taught to report after exercise?
back: Large or spreading bruises, blood in urine, black or bloody stools, nosebleeds that will not stop, a new severe headache, or a joint that becomes hot and swollen. Any head injury needs urgent medical assessment.

front: In hemophilia, what is the first-line plan for a suspected acute joint bleed (hemarthrosis) during therapy?
back: Stop activity, apply rest, ice, compression and elevation, and contact the hemophilia team for factor replacement as soon as possible. Do not stretch, massage, or resist the joint. Restart gently only after medical clearance.

front: Which symptoms during exercise in a client with anemia mean you should stop and reassess?
back: Disproportionate shortness of breath, dizziness, chest pain, palpitations, or a heart rate far above expected for the effort. Low oxygen-carrying capacity limits tolerance, so use RPE and the talk test and progress slowly.

front: What is the usual minimum turning interval for a bed-bound client at risk of pressure injury on a standard mattress?
back: At least every 2 hours, individualized to skin condition, comfort, and the support surface used. Document the schedule and check bony prominences each turn for non-blanchable redness, which signals early injury.

front: Why is 30-degree side-lying preferred over 90-degree side-lying for pressure injury prevention?
